text:
In 16 years, Nigeria has had four presidents. Yar'Adua, Jonathan, Buhari and Tinubu. But what is happening under Bola Ahmed Tinubu should genuinely worry every Nigerian who understands that government loans are debts our children will inherit.

Jonathan left Nigeria with a public debt of about ₦12.6 trillion in 2015. Buhari took over and, by the time he left in 2023, the country was already drowning in debt. The figure eventually reached ₦87.38 trillion in June 2023.

Then came Tinubu, the man who told Nigerians that subsidy was gone, who promised that the sacrifices of ordinary citizens would rescue the economy.

Three years later, where is the rescue?

Petrol subsidy was removed. Electricity tariffs increased. The naira collapsed. The cost of living became unbearable. Nigerians were told to endure hardship because the government needed money to develop the country.

Yet the borrowing never stopped.

By June 2026, Nigeria's public debt had reportedly climbed to ₦166.79 trillion. That is nearly ₦80 trillion above the June 2023 figure.

Now ask yourself, what exactly has the average Nigerian gained from all these sacrifices?

Where are the new industries? Where are the functioning hospitals? Where are the affordable universities? Where are the roads, electricity and employment opportunities that should justify this mountain of debt?

And then there is the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway.

A multitrillion-naira project awarded to Hitech Construction, a company associated with Gilbert Chagoury, a businessman with longstanding ties to President Tinubu.

The contract was awarded without an open competitive bidding process. Imagine committing such enormous public resources to a project of this magnitude without allowing companies to compete transparently for the job.

What exactly was the government afraid of discovering through competitive bidding? A cheaper contractor? A better offer? Or a process that would have subjected the entire arrangement to greater public scrutiny?

Even more disturbing is the controversy surrounding the Lagos corridor, where construction delays and questions about the project's continuation have raised serious concerns.

Nigerians deserve to know how much has been paid, how much work has actually been completed, and whether the original Lagos-to-Calabar promise will ever be fulfilled.

You cannot announce a coastal highway stretching across several states, commit trillions to it, and expect citizens to remain silent when the visible progress fails to match the political publicity.

And while all this is happening, the same government is budgeting trillions of naira to service debts.

Think about the madness of it.

We removed subsidy because the government claimed it could no longer afford it, yet we can afford questionable procurement arrangements, expensive political offices and an ever-expanding debt burden.

The ordinary Nigerian pays more for fuel, more for electricity, more for food, more for education and more in taxes. Meanwhile, the government keeps borrowing in the name of that same Nigerian.

At what point does sacrifice become exploitation?

At what point do we stop calling this economic reform and start demanding evidence of what the reforms have actually achieved?

If Tinubu believes his borrowing is necessary, let his administration publish a comprehensive account of every major loan contracted since May 2023, the projects financed, the contractors paid, the amounts disbursed and the repayment schedules.

Let Nigerians see the physical evidence.

Because borrowing money is not an achievement. Announcing contracts is not development. Removing subsidies is not economic competence.

And a president who demands endless sacrifice from the poor should be prepared to account for every naira spent by his government.

What is the point of removing the burden of subsidy from Nigerians only to replace it with a mountain of debt that their children and grandchildren will spend decades repaying?

text:
The claim that “Peter Obi built nothing in Anambra” is misleading and, on the evidence, false.

Peter Obi served as governor of Anambra State from 2006 to 2014 (with interruptions from court challenges). Political debate has long reduced his record to slogans. Independent fact-checks, contemporary news reports, policy assessments, and Obi’s own statements show substantial investment in education and health infrastructure, even if his approach in education prioritized upgrading and equipping existing facilities over constructing entirely new standalone schools.

Education: Upgrading Existing Infrastructure, Not New Schools from Scratch

Obi has publicly acknowledged that he did not build entirely new schools. In April 2024, responding to a challenge from Reno Omokri (who offered $10,000 for evidence of a school started, completed, and commissioned under Obi), he stated that his priority was fixing a system in collapse. When he took office, schools had been shut for extended periods, and Anambra ranked near the bottom nationally (around 26th in WAEC/NECO). He argued that “building new schools when the old ones are moribund is just like building coastal lines when internal roads are impassable.” By the end of his tenure, the state had risen to first place in national WAEC and NECO rankings, a turnaround documented in contemporary assessments and later policy papers.

Available records show significant physical and equipment investments inside and around existing schools:

- Classroom construction and rehabilitation: A 2017 THISDAY review of his achievements noted construction of classroom blocks. A February 2018 policy assessment (“Anambra State Education Rebirth – The Peter Obi Model”) reported that in 2012 the state projected 4,000 new classrooms, of which 1,000 had been completed (with more scheduled). Some accounts from supporters cite five-classroom blocks across Anambra’s 177 communities as part of a large-scale program. Funds were also released directly to schools (including mission schools) for renovations and new works; in 2013 alone, billions were disbursed for infrastructure upgrades under programs such as the World Bank-supported State Education Programme Investment Project (SEPIP).
- School buses: Channels Television reported in October 2013 that Obi distributed 500 brand-new buses to secondary schools (public and private) under the Millennium Development Goals scheme. Other contemporary and later accounts put the total higher (over 700 in one 2017 review).
- Technology and Microsoft Academies: The administration established Microsoft IT Academies in hundreds of secondary schools (reports range from an initial target of 100 to later figures of 450+). This involved large-scale distribution of computers/laptops (figures cited in the tens of thousands, including HP consignments), printers, internet connectivity, and generators so the equipment could function. One 2013 Vanguard report described a major agreement involving roughly ₦2.65 billion for ICT education, teacher training, and equipment across schools.
- Other support: Boreholes in hundreds of schools, funding for sick bays (including ₦525 million released directly in one instance), laboratory equipment for hundreds of schools, return of mission schools to their original church proprietors (with multi-billion-naira grants while the state continued paying teachers), and major development of the Igbariam permanent site of the state university (clearing bush, building faculties, library, and related infrastructure, plus a ₦5 billion intervention announced in 2013).

Healthcare: Clearer Evidence of New and Major Facilities

In health, the record includes both upgrades and new specialized facilities:

- Joseph Nwilo (Joe Nwiloh) Heart Centre: At St. Joseph’s Hospital, Adazi-Nnukwu. Obi’s administration funded and developed this center in partnership with the Catholic Diocese of Awka, naming it after the Anambra-born US cardiac surgeon Dr. Joseph Nwiloh. Contemporary reports (including This Day in 2012) show the governor releasing funds (e.g., ₦10 million cheques) for continued work. The centre enabled the first open-heart surgeries in Anambra around 2014, performed by Nwiloh’s team. It remains a reference point for specialized cardiac care in the Southeast.
- Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University Teaching Hospital (COOUTH), Awka (Amaku): Multiple sources, including contemporary reporting and Obi’s later statements, describe the transformation of the former Amaku General Hospital into the state’s first teaching hospital and associated College of Medicine. Over 20 new structures (clinics, laboratories, wards) were built. Obi has repeatedly stated it was delivered rapidly (claims of under two years or around 18 months) to meet Medical and Dental Council requirements after the medical school faced shutdown for lack of a teaching hospital, allowing existing medical students to continue. It is widely described as built or developed from the ground up during his tenure and remains the main state teaching hospital.
- Other facilities: Reports document new general hospitals in places such as Anaku and Umueri, renovations and equipment upgrades across existing hospitals, and substantial funding partnerships with mission hospitals (Iyienu Ogidi, Our Lady of Lourdes Ihiala, St. Charles Borromeo Onitsha, Holy Rosary, and others). Some of these later gained higher status or teaching-hospital roles. Accreditations of health institutions rose markedly (from near zero or very few to a dozen or more by 2014, covering nursing, midwifery, and related fields). Additional items include maternal and child centres, the state’s first public dialysis machine in Onitsha, and related infrastructure.

NewsVerifierAfrica’s fact-check of the broader “did not build schools and hospitals” claim (linked in part to statements by Lagos Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu) rated it misleading/false, noting the education focus on revitalization that produced ranking gains and the health-sector construction of new or substantially expanded facilities (including the Amaku transformation and new general hospitals).

Obi’s administration prioritised rehabilitating and equipping a dilapidated existing education system—classroom blocks, buses, computers/Microsoft Academies, boreholes, mission-school support—and achieved a documented rise to the top of national exam rankings. In health, there is clearer evidence of new specialized infrastructure (the Heart Centre and the state teaching hospital developed with many new structures) plus upgrades, new general hospitals, and accreditations.

Nigeria is OK.

Only Peter Obi can do it.

Vote Peter Obi/Kwankwaso

$SVV Q3 2026 earnings: Savers raises its profit plan but trims its sales outlook

The thrift-store chain Savers Value Village is selling more in America, while Canadian shoppers return slowly. Sales grew 9% excluding currency moves, four-fifths of it from American stores. Chief executive Mark Walsh said new stores 'ramp ahead of our original expectations'. It lifted its profit floor and trimmed its sales ceiling.

• Sales, before currency changes: +𝟖.𝟗% (+8.5% as reported)
• Profit before interest, tax and depreciation, excluding one-offs: $𝟕𝟓.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+8% from a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟏𝟔 ($0.14 a year ago)
• Full-year sales outlook: $𝟏.𝟕𝟕-𝟏.𝟕𝟖 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (middle of the range: 5.7% growth)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The standing case got better: the earnings plan moved up while only the sales ceiling came down. By our math the fourth quarter carries a percentage point of margin expansion, which finance chief Michael Maher called 'a key inflection point'. One caution: Canadian profit grew faster than sales, and he says that pace will not repeat.

The question now is whether ThriftIQ's pricing gains survive the jump from a hundred stores to the whole chain. It either becomes a lasting margin lever, or it merely makes pricing consistent and the early gain fades as every store adopts it. The 2027 margin plan arriving with the fourth-quarter results will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Savers Value Village runs 384 thrift stores in the United States, Canada and Australia, selling donated clothes and housewares. Profit before interest, tax and depreciation, excluding one-offs, reached $75.9 million, 8% above a year ago. Chief executive Mark Walsh called that a 'fourth consecutive quarter of year-over-year adjusted EBITDA growth'.

Reported figures flatter the comparison, because a year ago the chain wrote off refinancing costs and took store write-downs. Operating income rose 25%; by our math the gain is nearer 10% once those charges and this quarter's lease gain come out.

• Adjusted EBITDA: $75.9 million, from $70.0 million
• Net income: $23.4 million, against a $14.0 million loss
• Last year's store write-downs added back: $4.7 million
• This quarter's gain on ending store leases: $1.2 million

What to watch: the margin on that profit measure in the fourth quarter, which Michael Maher, the finance chief, expects 'to expand modestly'. A reading near last year's 16.0% would mean the cost savings went into opening stores instead of into margin.

🟢 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐆𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐬
Nearly everything Savers sells arrives as a donation, so what the chain pays for supply sets its margin. The cost of merchandise sold fell to 43.1% of sales from 44.1%, helped by more donations arriving at the stores' own collection centres and at GreenDrop stations nearby.

Those two channels supplied 82.4% of the pounds processed, against 80.7% a year ago, and they cost less per pound under the contracts with charity partners. Each pound also earned more retail sales, at $1.53, which Maher put down to 'exceptional sales yield growth, especially in Canada'.

What to watch: the donation share in the next quarterly filing. Savers opens stores with a donation mix well below the fleet average, so quick expansion drags the number down even as older stores improve.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐒𝐨𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐝
Savers opened nine stores in the quarter, including its first in Tennessee. Walsh said new stores 'ramp ahead of our original expectations' on profit, helped by pricing software that cuts 'the time required to train new graders by roughly half'.

Opening costs still weigh: pre-opening expense came to $5.1 million. American segment profit grew 16% even so, and its margin widened by 0.7 of a percentage point. Maher puts the lift a younger store base gives the American comparable sales number at about half a point.

What to watch: the seven openings planned for the fourth quarter and whether the year ends near 25. Walsh said Savers can hold this pace 'for years to come', so a shortfall would carry weight.

🟢 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐈𝐐 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐈𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝟏𝟎𝟖 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬
ThriftIQ is the chain's own pricing software, which sets the price of each donated item from a database covering 45,000 brands. It now runs in 108 stores and has priced more than 40 million items. That is about twice as many as in the spring.

Stores using it sell more units and earn higher sales yields at prices the same or lower than the rest of the fleet, and Maher said 'that gap has widened since last quarter'. He also warned that 'the actual benefit to the overall business thus far is still relatively small'.

What to watch: whether those economics hold as the software reaches every store by early 2028, because the three-year margin target leans on it. Sceptics read the gains as pricing consistency that thins at scale.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐚'𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Canada is the older half of the business, with 172 stores and shoppers who pulled back as living costs rose. Comparable sales there grew 1.5%, better than the spring quarter, and Walsh said the 'lower household income cohort showed growth' after sitting out earlier quarters.

Profit tells a different story from sales. Canadian segment profit rose 10%, to $49.9 million. Its margin widened 2.1 percentage points, almost all of that from tighter control of how much stock the stores process.

That is the awkward part of the turnaround framing. Maher told investors: 'You're not going to see that kind of improvement every single year.' For the fourth quarter the chain plans Canadian comparable sales only in the low single digits.

What to watch: Canadian segment profit in the fourth quarter, set against a base that already carries this year's efficiency gains. Growth from there would show the improvement is structural rather than a one-time harvest.

🔴 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧
Sales at American stores the chain has run for more than a year grew 5.9%, and that measure has held at mid-single digits or better for eight quarters. The comparison now gets harder: Maher said Savers is 'now lapping the strongest quarter in the recent history of the company in the U. S.'

For the fourth quarter the plan puts American comparable growth in the low to mid-single digits. By our math the full-year range leaves fourth-quarter sales about 1% under last year, or some 6% above it once the extra trading week comes out.

What to watch: the American comparable number for the fourth quarter. At the bottom of that range the full-year target of 3.5% to 4.0% comes under pressure.

🔴 𝐀𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠
Besides its shops, Savers sells goods it cannot use to textile traders and runs 19 stores in Australia. It reports the two together under the label Other. Their combined profit fell 23%, to $6.6 million, while sales there grew.

Over nine months that line has lost $7.1 million of profit, which cancels more than half of the $13.3 million gain in the chain's adjusted earnings. Neither Walsh nor Maher gave the decline a number in their prepared remarks, and the quarterly filing offers no cause.

What to watch: the Other profit line in the fourth-quarter segment table. Another fall of that size would mean the retail gains keep leaking away through wholesale pricing or Australia.

🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐈𝐬 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
Savers borrowed heavily before its listing and still owes $674.4 million, against $60.1 million of cash. It repaid $51.9 million during the quarter out of cash on hand, and an August prepayment cleared every remaining compulsory instalment on the term loan.

Net debt now sits at 2.3 times adjusted earnings, and Maher repeated the aim of 'a net leverage ratio under 2x by the end of next year'. In the same quarter the chain spent $10.0 million buying a million of its own shares, so cash travels two ways at once.

What to watch: debt at the year end, and how much of the $21.7 million left on the buy-back authorisation gets used. Faster repayment would show which priority wins when cash is short.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐀𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 $𝟏𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬
Savers announced Autotagger and image capture, machines that cut the handling each donated item needs. Maher put the benefit at 'annualized labor savings of approximately $10 million' once the rollout finishes, against 'approximately $40 million in CapEx over the next couple of years'. Both figures sit inside the margin plan management set out last quarter, which still has next year at the lower end.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟒.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Depreciation and amortisation reached $24.8 million, 35% more than a year ago. The charge now absorbs 5.4% of sales and has risen through the year as new stores, offsite processing sites and software come into use. That is why reported operating profit grows more slowly than the profit measure Maher highlights.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝟑𝟗 𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐤𝐬): $𝟏𝟕𝟐.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Cash from operations over nine months reached $172.1 million, more than double last year's figure. Two one-off items explain most of the jump: the chain paid $35.8 million less in tax, including a federal refund, and $27.6 million less in interest. Working capital also turned helpful.

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒𝟔.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Inventories ended the quarter at $46.9 million, slightly below a year ago, even though sales grew 8.5%. The chain added 20 stores over the same period, so stock per store fell. Donated goods are priced to clear, so a flat level suggests the sales floor keeps up with what processing sends it.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Net interest cost fell by a third, to $11.3 million. The average rate on borrowings dropped to 6.22% from 8.78% after last autumn's refinancing, and a June amendment cut the term loan's margin again. For the full year the company plans about $48 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: $𝟏.𝟕𝟕 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏.𝟕𝟖 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $1.77 billion to $1.79 billion
Narrowed. Savers kept the floor and took $10 million off the ceiling. That puts full-year growth near 5.7%, and by our math fourth-quarter sales about 1% under last year. Excluding the extra trading week in last year's fourth quarter, the comparison instead rises about 6%. Maher put fourth-quarter growth at 'roughly flat compared to Q4 of last year'.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: 𝟑.𝟓% 𝐭𝐨 𝟒.𝟎%  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from 3.0% to 4.0%
Raised. The floor moved up half a point to 3.5%, against 4.1% delivered over nine months. That points to a slower fourth quarter, and Maher expects American comparable growth in the low to mid-single digits with Canada in the low single digits. It is the second increase in a row, each worth a quarter point at the middle of the range.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞: $𝟔𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟕𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐨𝐫 $𝟎.𝟒𝟑 𝐭𝐨 $𝟎.𝟒𝟕 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $67 million to $76 million, or $0.42 to $0.47 per diluted share
Narrowed. Both ends moved in, leaving the middle near $72 million against $22.6 million last year, when refinancing costs ate the result. By our math the fourth quarter then carries about $32 million. The plan assumes a tax rate near 28%, while tax over nine months took 31.7%.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞: $𝟕𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟖𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐨𝐫 $𝟎.𝟒𝟖 𝐭𝐨 $𝟎.𝟓𝟐 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $76 million to $85 million, or $0.47 to $0.53 per diluted share
Narrowed. The ceiling came down $2 million while the floor held, trimming the middle to about $79.5 million. Per share the middle is unchanged at $0.50. By our math the fourth quarter needs roughly $29 million, a fifth more than last year. Savers assumes no further buy-backs in the share count.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟐𝟕𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐𝟕𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $265 million to $275 million
Raised. The floor went up $5 million, which lifts the middle of the range about 6.6% above last year. By our math the fourth quarter then delivers near $77.7 million. That is a margin of roughly 16.9%, against 16.0% a year ago, the expansion Maher called 'a key inflection point'. Each of the last two revisions added $2.5 million at the middle.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟏𝟑𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏𝟒𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $125 million to $145 million
Raised. The floor rose $10 million, taking planned spending to about 7.9% of planned sales. Nine months absorbed $108.0 million, leaving the rest for the fourth quarter. By our math that remainder is near $32 million. Autotagger adds to this line over the next two years without changing the high single-digit share of sales Maher described.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟓  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Approximately 25
Unchanged. The chain still plans about 25 openings this year. Eighteen are already trading, and seven more come in the fourth quarter. More than 20 of the year's openings land in America, across 11 states. Walsh said Savers can keep this pace 'for years to come'.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐈𝐐 𝐚𝐝𝐝 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧?
Maher says the benefit so far is 'still relatively small' while the gap to other stores widens. A figure for the whole fleet, in gross profit or margin, would show whether the pilot results scale.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐀𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐤𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠?
That line has shed $7.1 million of profit over nine months and cancels much of the retail gain. Neither executive addressed it in prepared remarks for a second quarter running.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧?
Canadian margin widened 2.1 points on a 1.5% sales gain. Maher says that scale of yearly improvement will not repeat, so investors need the size of what is left to harvest.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦?
Management repeats half a point to a full point of expansion a year from 2027, at the lower end next year. The starting base depends on a fourth quarter still to come.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐫𝐚 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰-𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬?
The spending floor rose $10 million while openings stayed near 25. Savers has not said what the added money buys, or what payback it now expects from a new store.

Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples : https://t.co/i2wRZ7UtGs

Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
Md Mahmudur RahmanMiner School of Computer and Information Sciences, Kennedy College of Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Lowell, USAAtqiya Munawara MahiMiner School of Computer and Information Sciences, Kennedy College of Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Lowell, USANazim Ahmed BelabbaciMiner School of Computer and Information Sciences, Kennedy College of Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Lowell, USAMohammad Arif Ul AlamMiner School of Computer and Information Sciences, Kennedy College of Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Lowell, USADepartment of Computer Systems Technology, North Carolina Agriculture and Technical Universitymalam7@ncat.eduAbstract
Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 μL droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, continuous wavelet transform, support vector machine, plasma, SARS-CoV-2keywords

1Introduction
Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) offers a multielemental approach to characterizing biological specimens through their atomic and ionic emission spectra. A focused laser pulse ablates a small amount of material and generates a transient plasma, whose emission provides information about the elemental composition of the interrogated sample [1]. The ability to acquire multiple elemental signatures from small sample volumes, with comparatively limited chemical preparation, has motivated applications in biological and biomedical analysis [2]. For complex biofluids, however, the analytical value of LIBS depends on more than detecting emission lines: it also requires spectral representations that preserve useful sample differences while limiting the influence of background emission, measurement variability, and matrix effects.Blood plasma is a particularly challenging matrix because its spectra reflect contributions from endogenous constituents, specimen preparation, and the conditions under which the laser-induced plasma is formed. Emission intensity cannot generally be interpreted as elemental concentration without accounting for excitation conditions, ablation behavior, and matrix-dependent effects [1, 2]. Drying a specimen on a solid substrate further introduces potential variability associated with deposition morphology and substrate emission. Consequently, identifying spectral features associated with sample labels requires careful distinction between biological variation and variation introduced during preparation or acquisition. This distinction is especially relevant when classification models are developed from relatively small collections of biological specimens.Previous studies have established the feasibility of combining LIBS with statistical learning for biological sample discrimination. Applications include the classification of protein biomarker solutions [3], discrimination of plasma samples from healthy and ovarian cancer-prone mice [4], and investigations of Alzheimer’s disease using LIBS and machine learning [5]. These studies motivate the use of multivariate spectral patterns in biomedical analysis, while also emphasizing the need to establish the analytical basis and generalizability of observed discrimination. A spectral feature associated with a disease-labeled group is not, by itself, evidence of a disease-specific biomarker.SARS-CoV-2-associated plasma samples provide a relevant setting for investigating these methodological questions. Molecular and antigen tests assess viral targets, whereas LIBS-based analysis of plasma examines spectral patterns that may reflect host-associated compositional differences. These approaches therefore address different analytical signals. Berlo et al. demonstrated that LIBS combined with machine learning could distinguish plasma from donors who had previously tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction from control plasma [6]. Their findings establish an important precedent for the present application. Further methodological evaluation should therefore address how spectral information is represented and used for classification, rather than assume that classification performance alone establishes direct viral detection or clinical diagnostic validity.Feature extraction is central to this problem. Full LIBS spectra contain numerous correlated variables, while potentially informative differences may be concentrated within a smaller set of emission features. With limited numbers of independent specimens, the choice of spectral representation can influence both classification performance and the interpretation of the resulting model. Continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based peak detection uses localized responses across spectral scales to identify candidate peaks; wavelet-based methods have previously been investigated for analytical peak detection [7]. The resulting spectral representation depends on peak structure, background variation, and peak-detection https://t.co/UtMaUQVSsk this study, we evaluate CWT-based peak detection for the classification of human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. The dataset comprises 181 individual specimens, including 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls. Spectra were acquired from dried plasma droplets on silicon substrates, and the extracted peak features were used to train an SVM classifier. The evaluation focuses on classification performance under the reported leave-one-out cross-validation procedure, the emission features retained by the peak-based representation, and the effects of selected wavelength exclusions and wavelet settings.The contribution of this work is an evaluation of CWT-based spectral peak extraction within a specimen-level LIBS classification workflow. Using plasma specimens labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative, we examine the resulting classification performance, the sensitivity of peak selection to wavelet settings, and the effects of selected wavelength exclusions. The analysis is intended to characterize the behavior of the spectral representation within the available specimen collection; independent validation is required to establish its generalizability.Plasma specimen collectionRound 1: 118 specimens (24 positive, 94 negative)Round 2: 63 specimens (29 positive, 34 negative)↓Combined LIBS cohort181 individuals: 53 positive, 128 negative controls↓Specimen preparation5 μL plasma on silicon; infrared drying for 10 min↓LIBS acquisition1064 nm Nd:YAG laser; 100 single-shot spectra per specimen↓Within-specimen preprocessingReject spectra outside mean ± 1 SD of total emission intensityAverage retained spectra↓Specimen-level LIBS datasetCWT–SVM analysisFigure 1:Plasma specimen collection, preparation, and LIBS data acquisition. Two collection rounds yielded 181 specimens, comprising 53 SARS-CoV-2-positive samples and 128 negative controls. Following deposition and drying on silicon substrates, 100 single-shot spectra were acquired per specimen. Spectra with total emission intensities outside the within-specimen mean ± one standard deviation were excluded, and retained spectra were averaged for subsequent CWT-SVM analysis. Sample counts refer to individual specimens rather than laser shots.

2Datasets

2.1Blood Plasma LIBS Spectra Sample Collection and Initial Signal Processing
A total of 181 human plasma specimens were collected in sodium citrate anticoagulant from donors drawn by MRN Diagnostics both before (pre 11/2019) and after the appearance of SARS-CoV-2 in the United States. Informed consent was obtained from all subjects and studies were performed in accordance with FDA guidelines and regulations including IRB approval. Specimens were collected in two rounds: in the first round, 118 samples were collected (24 SARS-CoV-2 ‘positive’ and 94 ‘negative’ control) and in the second round, 63 samples were collected (29 SARS-CoV-2 ‘positive’ and 34 ‘negative’ control) samples. The 181 samples provided by MRN Diagnostics were analyzed by University of Massachusetts using LIBS technology.Prior to performing LIBS measurements of the blood plasma samples, 5 μL of each individual blood plasma specimen were deposited on the unpolished side of pure S​i wafers. These wafers were previously rinsed in 2-propanol. The blood plasma samples deposited on the S​i wafers were then dried for 10 min using a Tungsten infrared lamp. During the laser ablation process, separate single-shot spectra were captured from adjacent spots within the deposited droplet.The experimental setup for LIBS involved focusing 7 ns Nd:YAG laser pulses (Surelite II, Continuum) with a wavelength of 1064 nm onto the samples using an air-spaced doublet lens with a focal length of 30 mm. The blood plasma specimens were loaded onto a computer-controlled translation stage within a SciTrace chamber (AtomTrace), and the emission from the laser-induced plasma was collected using a 50 μm core-diameter optical fiber positioned at a 45∘ angle relative to the laser beam. The optical fiber was connected to an Echelle spectrograph (Andor Technology, ME 5000) and a thermoelectrically cooled iStar Intensified Charge Coupled Device (ICCD) camera (Andor Technology, DH734-18F-03). The time parameters utilized for this work were as follows: a gate delay of 1 microsecond and a gate width of 5 microseconds. The focused laser spot had a diameter of approximately 100 μm, operating at a repetition rate of 1 Hz with a laser energy of 130±2 mJ. All measurements were conducted in ambient air pressure. For each blood plasma sample, a total of 100 single-shot spectra were collected. Each spectrum was obtained from a new location on the dried blood plasma drop by using the 3-D translation stage after each laser shot. During analysis, the 100 individual spectra obtained for each sample were averaged, with any outlier spectra - those falling outside the range of mean ±1 standard deviation of total emission intensity - being excluded from the average process.📷Figure 2:Median specimen-level LIBS intensities in the positive (green) and negative (red) groups at selected wavelengths. Error bars indicate the first and third quartiles. The horizontal axis shows wavelength in nanometers.

3Methods

3.1Analytical workflow and unit of analysis
The analysis combined continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak detection with support vector machine (SVM) classification. Specimen preparation, LIBS acquisition, and intensity-based rejection of individual laser-shot spectra are described in the preceding section. Following these procedures, the retained spectra were averaged within each specimen to obtain one representative spectrum per individual. The individual specimen, rather than the laser shot, was the unit of analysis.The resulting dataset comprised 181 specimen-level spectra, including 53 specimens labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive and 128 negative controls. The analytical workflow consisted of detecting candidate emission peaks, aligning their wavelength positions across specimens, constructing peak-intensity feature vectors, and classifying the specimens using an SVM. Classification was evaluated against the supplied specimen labels.
3.2Continuous wavelet transform for spectral peak detection
CWT-based peak detection was used to identify localized features in the specimen-level LIBS spectra. Wavelet methods characterize spectral structure by comparing the measured signal with translated and scaled versions of a reference function, providing a basis for detecting peaks over a range of characteristic widths [7, 8].Let fi​(t) denote the averaged emission intensity of specimen i at spectral coordinate t. Its continuous wavelet transform is expressed asWi​(u,s)=1s​∫−∞+∞fi​(t)​ψ∗​(t−us)​𝑑t,s>0,(1)where u is the translation parameter, s is the scale parameter, ψ is the mother wavelet, and the asterisk denotes complex conjugation. The transform was applied to the discretely sampled spectra. Spectral coordinates were associated with their measured wavelengths for subsequent peak alignment and interpretation.A Mexican-hat wavelet was used because its central positive lobe and flanking negative lobes provide a localized representation of peak-like structure. A normalized form isψ⁡(t)=23​π1/4​(1−t2)​exp⁡(−t22).(2)This real-valued wavelet has zero mean and is proportional to the negative second derivative of a Gaussian. Translation determines the position at which the spectrum is examined, whereas scale controls the characteristic width of the structure to which the wavelet responds.Candidate peaks were identified from the wavelet response and screened using a signal-to-noise criterion. The retained peak positions were then associated with their intensities in the specimen-level spectrum. Figure 3 illustrates the resulting peak detections.📷Figure 3:Illustration of CWT-based peak detection in a specimen-level LIBS spectrum. The blue curve represents the measured spectrum, and red markers indicate retained peak positions.

3.3Peak alignment and feature construction
Detected peaks were aligned by wavelength to establish corresponding spectral features across specimens. This alignment provided a common feature representation in which each column corresponded to a matched peak position and each row corresponded to an individual specimen. For p aligned features, the feature vector for specimen i was𝐱i=(xi​1,xi​2,…,xi​p)𝖳,(3)where xi​j denotes the spectral peak height assigned to feature j in specimen i. The complete feature matrix was 𝐗∈ℝN×p, with N=181. The response variable was yi=1 for a positive specimen and yi=0 for a negative control.Peak heights were treated as empirical spectral descriptors. They were not converted to elemental concentrations, and their association with specimen labels was not interpreted as evidence of disease-specific elemental biomarkers.
3.4Support vector machine classification
An SVM was used to classify specimens from their aligned peak-intensity vectors [9, 10]. The reported analysis examined linear and nonlinear kernels and selected a radial basis function (RBF) kernel. For feature vectors 𝐱i and 𝐱j, the RBF kernel isK⁡(𝐱i,𝐱j)=exp⁡(−γ​‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖22),(4)where γ>0 determines the kernel width. The regularization parameter C controls the trade-off between the margin penalty and classification errors. The reported CWT-SVM configuration used C=10−3.
3.5Cross-validation and performance measures
The reported classification analysis used leave-one-out cross-validation at the specimen level. In each iteration, one specimen was withheld for evaluation and the remaining 180 specimens were used for classifier training. This procedure was repeated until every specimen had served once as the evaluation case. The procedure therefore assessed internal predictive performance within the available specimen collection.For evaluation, positive specimens were designated as the positive class. Classification performance is defined from the pooled out-of-fold class predictions asAccuracy=T​P+T​NT​P+T​N+F​P+F​N,(5)Sensitivity=T​PT​P+F​N,(6)Specificity=T​NT​N+F​P,(7)where T​P, T​N, F​P, and F​N denote the numbers of true-positive, true-negative, false-positive, and false-negative predictions, respectively. Values are expressed as percentages in the results.
3.6Peak-detection settings and wavelength-exclusion analysis
The influence of peak-detection settings was examined by varying the signal-to-noise criterion and wavelet width. The resulting peak selections were compared to assess how these parameters affected the retention of weak features and the separation of neighboring peaks. text:
The Talks Are Not About Stopping the War. The War Is the Cover for the Talks.

Read the guest list again. Steve Witkoff, a real estate developer. Jared Kushner, whose firm holds $2 billion from the Saudi PIF plus money from Lunate and Qatari entities. The UAE Foreign Minister, representing a state that hosts Al Dhafra Air Base and Jebel Ali port and whose adviser said "confidence has been shaken."

None of these men are negotiating an end to the fighting. They are negotiating the title deed to the reconstruction. The war continues on the battlefield because the war is the pressure mechanism that forces the asset transfer. A ceasefire is not the goal. A ceasefire is the closing condition.

What Is Actually Being Divided

The minerals. The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, signed 30 April 2025, gives the United States a 50 per cent share of revenue from every newly issued mineral, oil, and gas extraction licence. Managed jointly by the US International Development Finance Corporation and Ukraine's PPP Agency. Trump, July 2026: "We can go in there at any time we want to take pretty much whatever we want."

The fund has no security guarantee. It has no reconstruction obligation. It has a claim on the revenue.

The frozen assets. Roughly €210 billion at Euroclear in Belgium. The EU has taxed the windfall profits at 99.7 per cent. A €90 billion loan has been approved with two-thirds for weapons. Belgium is blocking outright confiscation, citing international law and Euroclear's exposure to Russian legal retaliation. The principal is immobilised. The legal basis for taking it is being constructed while the talks run.

The reconstruction contracts. Ukraine's infrastructure damage is estimated in the hundreds of billions. The contracts to rebuild it will be awarded by the same governments that are negotiating the ceasefire. The men at the table in Abu Dhabi are not discussing who will rebuild. They are discussing who will own the rebuild.

The Mechanism: Ceasefire as Closing Condition

A war that continues is a war that cannot be monetised. Investors do not buy reconstruction bonds in an active war zone. The minerals fund does not generate revenue while the mines are under artillery. The frozen assets cannot be legally transferred while the war is running, because the legal justification for transfer depends on the war ending.

So the war must appear to be ending. That is what the Abu Dhabi talks produce. Not a ceasefire. A process. A photograph. A communiqué. A "framework" that allows the financial architecture to begin pricing the assets.

The war will continue on the ground. The artillery will keep firing. The casualties will keep mounting. But the legal fiction of a peace process will be established, and the asset transfer can proceed.

The Libya Precedent

In 2011, NATO bombed Libya into a failed state. Muammar Gaddafi was killed. The country collapsed into civil war. The oil was the prize. The reconstruction contracts were the follow-on. The slave markets in Tripoli were the by-product.

The men who ran that operation are the same men who are running this one. The same architecture. The same financial institutions. The same assumption that a destroyed state is a state whose assets can be acquired at a discount.

The Venezuela Precedent

The United States kidnapped Nicolás Maduro in January 2026. Delcy Rodríguez was installed as the client vice president. Marco Rubio stated the policy: "Venezuela will not be able to sell oil unless the United States decides to allow it."

The plan was to take 30 to 50 million barrels of Venezuelan oil and sell it at market price. Reliance Industries, owned by Mukesh Ambani, was the refinery that would process it. Jamnagar, the world's largest single-site refinery, was the valve.

Rubio flew to Jamnagar on 21 October 2026 to close the deal. The diesel prices his war had caused were the domestic political problem. The Venezuelan oil was the solution. The title deed was the point.

The Countries That Are Not at the Table

Iran is not in Abu Dhabi. The seven conditions published by the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces and Commander of the Khatm al-Anbiya Central Headquarters remain on file. Rezaei used the word "surrender." Baghaei compressed the timeline from seven days to two. Araghchi called the reports of a Reaei-Vance meeting "media fabrications."

Iran is not being offered a minerals deal. Iran is not being offered a reconstruction fund. Iran is being offered the seven conditions, and it is demanding that they be implemented fully and simultaneously.

The difference is the asset base. Ukraine has minerals. Ukraine has frozen Russian assets. Ukraine has a reconstruction bill. Iran has oil, gas, and a strait. The architecture can price Ukraine. It cannot price Iran, because Iran has not been defeated.

So the talks are in Abu Dhabi for Ukraine, and the war continues for Iran. The smokescreen is the peace process. The reality is the asset division.

The American Political File

Vance published a post-mortem admitting the war lost the election. Trump Jr. endorsed it. Rubio is leaving. Hegseth is under prediction of dismissal. Cooper is mocked as a podcast host.

The administration needs a win before the new Congress seats in January. The Abu Dhabi talks are the win. The communiqué will be the headline. The minerals fund will be the footnote. The €210 billion will be the paragraph nobody reads.

The Bill

Witkoff. Kushner. The UAE Foreign Minister. Two men with no diplomatic credentials. One state calculating its own exposure.

The minerals fund: 50 per cent of new Ukrainian extraction revenue. No security guarantee. No reconstruction obligation.

The frozen assets: €210 billion at Euroclear. 99.7 per cent windfall tax. €90 billion loan, two-thirds weapons. Belgium blocking confiscation.

The Libya precedent: 2011, NATO destroyed the state, the oil was the prize. The Venezuela precedent: 2026, Maduro kidnapped, Delcy Rodríguez installed, Rubio in Jamnagar with Ambani.

Iran is not at the table. The seven conditions remain. "Surrender," Rezaei's word. "Two days," Baghaei's deadline. "Media fabrications," Araghchi's phrase.

The talks are not about stopping the war. They are about who owns the wreckage. The war continues because the wreckage is not yet fully priced. The ceasefire is the closing condition. The peace process is the smokescreen. The bill is being paid by the dead, and the receipt is a communiqué from Abu Dhabi.

text:
🇦🇪|The Circus in Abu Dhabi: Three Men Who Owe Their Fortunes to the Gulf Are Negotiating a War They Have No Mandate to End.

The table in Abu Dhabi has Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and the UAE Foreign Minister on one side. Read the guest list against the financial disclosure forms.

Who Is Sitting at the Table

Jared Kushner runs Affinity Partners. The firm's capital: $2 billion** from Saudi Arabia's **Public Investment Fund**, approved in **2021** over the objections of the PIF's own advisers. Add money from **Lunate**, an Abu Dhabi fund, and from Qatari sovereign entities. Kushner was the architect of the **Abraham Accords** and is the son-in-law of the President. He has no diplomatic credential beyond the family tie. He has a **$2 billion Gulf-funded investment firm and a seat at a table negotiating the fate of Ukraine.

Steve Witkoff is a real estate developer and Trump's golf partner. He has no diplomatic background. He was in Moscow meeting Vladimir Putin while the war was running. He was in the room when Trump spoke to Putin. He is not a career Foreign Service officer, not a regional specialist, not a treaty negotiator. He is a man whose qualification is a friendship.

The UAE Foreign Minister represents a state that hosts Al Dhafra Air Base (24.25°N 54.55°E), the US F-35 and ISR hub, and Jebel Ali port, the largest US military logistics node in the Gulf. The UAE is on the Zero Hour target list. An Emirati aircraft flew into Tehran and departed unannounced. Anwar Gargash, adviser to the President, said publicly: "Confidence has been shaken." The host of the talks is a state calculating its own exposure.

What They Are Actually Negotiating

Not the end of the war. The collateral.

The minerals deal signed in April 2025 gives the United States a 50 per cent share of revenue from every newly issued Ukrainian mineral, oil, and gas extraction licence, through a fund managed jointly by the US International Development Finance Corporation and Ukraine's PPP Agency. Trump's own description, July 2026: "We can go in there at any time we want to take pretty much whatever we want. That was a pretty good deal."

The frozen Russian assets: roughly €210 billion at Euroclear in Belgium. The EU has taxed the windfall profits at 99.7 per cent and transferred the proceeds to Kyiv. A €90 billion loan has been approved with two-thirds earmarked for weapons. Belgium has blocked outright confiscation, citing international law and Euroclear's exposure to Russian legal retaliation. The principal is immobilised. The legal basis for taking it is being constructed.

That is the negotiation. Who holds the claim on the minerals. Who takes the principal on the frozen assets. Who pays for the reconstruction. Ukraine is the collateral. The men at the table in Abu Dhabi are not negotiating Ukraine's future. They are negotiating the title deed.

The Precedent They Are Burying

The deal that would have ended the war was on the table in Istanbul in April 2022. Ukraine's written proposals included neutral, non-aligned status and a pledge not to host foreign weapons, including nuclear arms.

Boris Johnson flew to Kyiv on 9 April 2022. Yulia Mendel, Zelensky's former press secretary, said Johnson "intervened and influenced Zelensky, saying he could become a hero and could continue this war." David Arakhamia, head of the Ukrainian delegation, said Johnson told them: "We won't sign anything with them at all."

The neutrality that Witkoff and Kushner are now discussing was on offer four years ago. It was destroyed by a British prime minister acting on instructions from Washington and London. The men in Abu Dhabi are negotiating the terms that were available before hundreds of thousands of dead.

The Body Count Behind the Table

Zelensky: 50,000 Ukrainian soldiers killed, down from 55,000 he cited earlier, a revision in the wrong direction for a casualty count.

The Economist: 1.4 to 2.1 million Russian casualties, 374,000 to 770,000 killed.

CSIS: 1.4 million Russian casualties, 400,000 to 450,000 killed, and a ratio of Russian to Ukrainian losses in the first half of 2026 of roughly 8 to 1.

Mediazona: 7,983 named Russian officers confirmed dead by 6 November 2026.

Total: upwards of 2 million casualties between the two armies.

The men negotiating in Abu Dhabi did not pay that bill. The Ukrainians and the Russians did.

The American Political File

JD Vance published a post-mortem admitting the war lost the midterms, quoting his own pollster's finding that the top four reasons Trump 2024 voters abandoned the ticket were end the war, cost of living, America First, and change the relationship with Israel. Donald Trump Jr. reposted it: "Every word of this is 100% correct."

Marco Rubio is reportedly preparing to resign and run for president, separating his brand from the war. While those reports circulated, he was in Jamnagar, Gujarat on 21 October, meeting Mukesh Ambani about routing Venezuelan crude through Reliance's refinery to fix the diesel prices the war caused.

Pete Hegseth is under prediction of dismissal from Mohsen Rezaei. Admiral Brad Cooper is mocked as a podcast host by the IRGC spokesman and the Foreign Ministry.

An administration that lost both chambers over the war, whose officials are leaving or under prediction of removal, is now sending two men with no diplomatic credentials to negotiate the end of that war in a Gulf capital that hosts the base the war runs from.

The Venue Is the Tell

Abu Dhabi is not Geneva. It is not Vienna. It is not a neutral capital with a treaty secretariat and a permanent negotiating team.

Abu Dhabi is a Gulf monarchy that hosts US bases, that is on the Zero Hour target list, whose adviser said "confidence has been shaken," and whose aircraft flew to Tehran unannounced. It is a state that is renegotiating its own exposure while hosting the talks that will determine whether the war ends.

The UAE is not mediating. The UAE is protecting itself.

The Bill

Witkoff. Kushner. The UAE Foreign Minister. Three men. Two with no diplomatic credential. One representing a state calculating its own risk.

Affinity Partners: $2 billion from the Saudi PIF, plus Lunate and Qatari money. Kushner's firm. Kushner's seat.

The minerals deal: 50 per cent of new Ukrainian extraction revenue. Trump: "take pretty much whatever we want."

€210 billion at Euroclear. 99.7 per cent windfall tax. €90 billion loan, two-thirds weapons. Belgium blocking confiscation.

Istanbul 2022: the deal was on the table. Boris Johnson said no. Mendel and Arakhamia confirmed it.

2 million casualties between the armies. 50,000 Ukrainian dead per Zelensky. 7,983 named Russian officers per Mediazona.

Vance conceded. Trump Jr. endorsed it. Rubio leaving. Hegseth predicted to fall. Cooper a podcast host.

The circus is in Abu Dhabi because the men who run it cannot hold the show in a capital where they would have to answer questions. The negotiators owe their fortunes to the Gulf. The venue owes its security to the bases. The deal is the title deed. The bill was paid by the dead. Khallas.
