text:
@MayorToddGloria, serious question. Why are we committing nearly 49 acres of valuable publicly owned land to a development where 2,000 of the 4,254 homes are income restricted, instead of aggressively competing to attract engineers, advanced manufacturing, technology companies, and highly paid professionals who could strengthen San Diego’s economy for generations?

I genuinely support redeveloping the Sports Arena property. But I question whether we’re thinking ambitiously enough about what this land could become.

San Diego already has extraordinary advantages in aerospace, defense, biotechnology, robotics, autonomous systems, and scientific research.

We should be building an economic environment that attracts the world’s best engineers, researchers, entrepreneurs, and innovative companies.

Imagine a modern district with high quality market rate apartments, beautiful public spaces, research facilities, engineering offices, technology startups, and businesses creating thousands of highly paid jobs.

Those workers would spend money locally, support restaurants and small businesses, generate economic activity, and contribute to a stronger tax base.

Instead, we’re dedicating approximately 47% of the proposed housing to income restricted units while allocating only a relatively small amount of space to commercial development.

I understand affordable housing serves working families, and those residents contribute to our economy too. But we need to distinguish helping individual households from maximizing the long term economic productivity of a uniquely valuable public asset.

Why not focus more aggressively on creating opportunities for San Diegans to earn higher incomes in the first place?

Why not attract employers that can offer careers in aerospace engineering, artificial intelligence, advanced robotics, biotechnology, and other industries with substantial growth potential?

Why not create a district that encourages new companies to establish headquarters, employ local graduates, and invest in San Diego?

I understand California law imposes affordable housing obligations on certain public land developments. But that still leaves an important question.

What is the legally required minimum, and what economic tradeoffs did the city evaluate before committing to 2,000 restricted units?

I would like to see a serious comparison between this proposal and alternatives with more market rate housing, substantially greater commercial activity, and dedicated space for high paying industries.

Show us the projected tax revenue, permanent employment, average wages, private investment, infrastructure expenses, and financial returns over the next 30 to 100 years.

Your administration projects thousands of permanent jobs from this development. What percentage will actually be high paying technical and professional positions, and how do those projections compare with other possible uses of the property?

I don’t want San Diego to become a city where we simply accept that ordinary residents cannot afford to live here and respond exclusively with income restricted housing.

I want us to become a city where far more residents can afford housing because we’ve created a stronger, more productive economy with substantially better career opportunities.

Affordable housing addresses one consequence of our economic challenges. Better education, stronger industries, greater productivity, and higher incomes address other parts of the problem.

Those objectives should be evaluated together.

San Diego has the talent, universities, defense presence, and geographic advantages to become an even more significant center of American engineering and technological innovation.

We should be thinking on that scale.

Mayor Gloria, can you demonstrate that the current agreement produces greater long term public value than a more commercially ambitious alternative?

If the numbers support your decision, publish the comparison

Taittiriya Brahmana (III.9.8.2–3): Explicitly states that the cow is food (atho annam vai gauh — “verily the cow is food”). It appears in the context of sacrifice, where binding the cow secures both the sacrifice and food for the sacrificer.
•  Satapatha Brahmana (III.1.2.21): Discusses restrictions on eating cow or ox flesh (because they support the world), but records the sage Yajnavalkya saying he eats it if it is tender. This shows both emerging caution and continued consumption by some Brahmins.
•  Rigveda: Multiple references to Indra consuming large numbers of oxen, bulls, or buffaloes (e.g., X.86.14: “they cook for me fifteen plus twenty oxen”). Cattle appear among animals offered in sacrifice, after which the meat was typically shared with the priests and participants.
•  Grhyasutras, Dharmasutras, and early Smritis (including references in Manusmriti and Yajnavalkya Smriti): Describe hospitality rites (madhuparka) and funerary rites (sraddha) in which ox or cow meat was offered to guests or Brahmins. Manusmriti recalls legendary Brahmins who ate ox or even dog meat in extreme need. Preference for beef in certain sraddha contexts is noted in the texts.

text:
The Bible’s understanding of Satan develops across centuries of Jewish and Christian history.

The Hebrew word satan (שָׂטָן) originally means adversary or accuser.

In Job, Satan appears in God’s heavenly court, not as God’s equal.

In Genesis, the serpent is never explicitly identified as Satan.

During the Second Temple period, Jewish writings developed more elaborate accounts of demons, rebellious angels, and cosmic evil.

The Dead Sea Scrolls describe a struggle between the forces of light and darkness.

Persian Zoroastrianism offers intriguing parallels, although direct influence remains debated.

By the New Testament, Satan is portrayed as a personal spiritual adversary.

The familiar story of Lucifer’s fall combines passages from Isaiah and Ezekiel that originally address earthly kings.

Traditional Judaism generally does not view Satan as an independent power equal to God.

The concept of the yetzer hara also locates the struggle against evil within human nature.

History documents the development of these beliefs, but cannot independently prove Satan’s supernatural existence.

So is Satan a spiritual adversary, the personification of evil, or both—and what if the greatest deception is making us mistake a lie for the truth?

text:
A. R. Rahman and Hans Zimmer’s wall-to-wall score in Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana (2026) is a seamless combination of the composers’ individual styles. More a brassy, bombastic score than one brimming with bhakti rasa (something the film isn’t going for either), though. The background score works incredibly well within the film and would be thoroughly entertaining as an extra-filmic listening experience once the original soundtrack album is released. There are at least 40 different musical cues in the score. Those who are familiar with the composers’ works can easily hear who composed what in the score. There are several cues that are entirely A. R. Rahman, some entirely Hans Zimmer, and some other cues where Zimmer and Rahman’s layers are in perfect harmony—for example, the Indian electric violin parts that find their space in between and over the phrases composed by Zimmer for Ram (can be heard in the track “Rama Theme”).

All the electric violin parts heard throughout the film (used for Dashanan’s Tapasya, Indra’s dive into the deep ocean, Bharat Milap sequence) are by A. R. Rahman. This is a brilliant choice; the instrument’s timbre is modest and muted compared to the traditional violin or sarangi (typically used in emotional sequences in such films) that even in high registers it doesn’t squeal, which might sound sappy and excessive to a Western audience (and a cello might sound too low and Western), and so it offers a perfect sonic solution for what the film is attempting here—to appeal to both Indian and international audiences. The distinct tone of this instrument is most pronounced in the Vanvas theme that is heard in the film when Ram, Sita, and Lakshman bid adieu to Dasarath and Kaikeyi in the throne room.

A. R. Rahman's rousing cry for Ram makes a moment in the leaving-for-exile episode pivotal (the film should have cut to intermission immediately after this episode). The film by itself does not earn the emotion an audience member might feel at this moment; the audiences’ past encounters with the story could do it instead, and A. R. Rahman’s high cosmic wail matches the register of this emotion. The visual in this sequence looks stunning on the big screen—the carriage lit in golden yellow passing through a sea of darkness, almost a painting.

Equally visually stunning is the moment when Ram meets Sita for the first time, a moment made all the more glorious by Rahman’s music. The ascending strings as Sita approaches the temple, the musicality of the Sanskrit verses themselves, the meditative melody the verses are set to, the musical conversation between male and female voices as Ram and Sita exchange glances, the rousing orchestral coda as Sita leaves—the spatio-temporal congruence and the emotional congruence between the music and the moving image in this sequence are magical.

There are several other cues that are entirely A. R. Rahman: a sweet female solo for Surpanakha who is now smitten by Ram; the music that plays in the Swayamvar sequence (music heard after Ram picks the bow is more Zimmer, a variation of the Rama theme)—the warm, whimsical, bouncy strings we hear as men fail to lift the bow (reminded me of the track “Shark” from Couples Retreat and the strings heard throughout the The Hundred-Foot Journey score); the orchestral version of the song "Jai Jai Ram" is played a few times in the film—when Dasarath makes Ram wear his crown and when a forest blooms and comes to life after Ram kills the giants whose spell the forest was under. While the melody of “Dharti hai ambar” is A. R. Rahman, the accompanying deafeningly gargantuan chorus and orchestral layers are typical Zimmer. In other moments, where there is chorus singing Sanskrit verses, for example, in the sequences where Ram fights the giants in the forest, the music is largely Rahman, even if entirely orchestral.

Ram and Ravan get distinct leitmotifs, the orchestral variations of which are heard throughout the film. The four-note Ravan motif is Zimmer, but there is a secondary theme, a low, grunting, rumbling male choir (singing some non-linguistic syllables) which is clearly Rahman and sounds derived from the track “Ravana Thandav.” And the thandav track is thunderous and effective within the film. The version played in the film’s prologue is much longer, with Zimmer’s Ravan theme dubbed over Rahman’s densely layered percussive Indian parts. This opening prologue is made all the more breathtaking by the accompanying score to which both Rahman and Zimmer seem to have contributed equally. There are several more interesting musical cues in the score. I can’t wait to listen to the original soundtrack album. Might watch the film again just to hear the score. For now, I’ll leave you with the beautiful Vanvas theme.

text:
Both non-Christian 2nd Temple Jewish literature (such as the Testament of Levi and 2 Enoch) and the New Testament (also 2nd Temple literature) envision multiple heavens: the first being that of the clouds, the second that of the heavenly bodies, the third being the realm of God and the angels. 

Whether one can call it a _physical_ realm is questionable: in Revelation, all that is required for John of Patmos to ascend into the third heaven is for a door to open directly to his location, so this realm is clearly not a physical location that is located _literally_ above the physical sky. Clearly you could go up to the third heaven without having to go through the first and second heavens. 

Jesus' ascension is not simply about travel, it is also a conqueror's march. Just as he descended into the realm of the dead to subjugate the powers of death, he ascended into the air to subjugate the rebellious powers of the air, and into the starry skies so he could subjugate the powers there, and the end goal was so that he could fill all things (Ephesians 4.8). 

In other words, Jesus even qua his humanity is somehow _everywhere_ in a way transcending spatial relations — and indeed, the very nature of the Eucharist as making Christ present everywhere the oblation is offered makes no sense without a kind of super-spatial (note how I still use a spatial metaphor) presence of Christ in all physical locations.

text:
CoRL 2026 Poster 🌟

Why can adding more first-person human video actually make a robot worse at a task?

Georgia Tech researchers found a problem with traditional behavior cloning.

Humans and robots see the world differently, have different bodies, and move in different ways.

When human videos are added to training, models can end up learning human motions that robots simply can't perform.

The team introduced EgoWAM to address this.

Instead of only predicting actions, it also trains robots to predict how the world changes after an action.

The team compared three ways to represent those changes:

• Pixel: Predicts future frames at the pixel level.

• DINO: Predicts semantic features extracted by a vision model, focusing on objects and scene content.

• 3D Motion Flow: Predicts how objects move in 3D space, separating camera motion from actual changes in the environment.

The team tested EgoWAM on three real-world bimanual tasks: placing a cup on a saucer, bagging groceries, and folding clothes.

The experiments involved 1,800 real-robot trials.

The results:

Pixel prediction offered limited gains.

DINO delivered the strongest OOD generalization.

Compared with robot-only training, it improved success rates by:
• 43 percentage points on cup placement.
• 40 points on grocery bagging.
• 70 points on clothes folding.

Clothes-folding success in OOD tests reached 85%.

3D Flow was better for precise spatial manipulation.

It improved in-domain success rates by:
• 20 percentage points on cup placement.
• 30 points on grocery bagging.
Both tasks reached 90% success.

On grocery bagging, 3D Flow also delivered a 45-point gain in OOD testing.

EgoWAM points to a different way of training robots.

text:
David J Harris Jr.: 
🇬🇧"Hello, I am Palestinian. 
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.
1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.
1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.
1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.
Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.
Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.
Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.
Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.
Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.
Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.
I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.
And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

What’s on the table in Abu Dhabi? Ukraine, Russia attempt the outlines of a new European security deal

The US-brokered Russia-Ukraine talks beginning in Abu Dhabi on November 10 may represent the best opportunity yet to end the war before Russian President Vladimir Putin completely destroys what is left of Ukraine’s economy. Kyiv is already almost totally blacked out and temperatures are just above freezing. A mass exodus from the capital is now on the cards.

There will be no breakthrough today – that’s not the plan. Unlike previous rounds, these talks have started with a pragmatic frame of mind: build a step-by-step process to get to settlement. The delegates are meeting to sketch out a wireframe of a potential deal, and a series of meetings are planned building up to a final Putin-Zelenskiy tête-à-tête when a final bargain could be struck.

But it’s going to be hard. Putin goes into the meeting under mild pressure as the Russian economy is feeling real pain now, but not enough to force his hand. Zelenskiy goes into the talks in a desperate situation: he has run out of defence ammo completely; his corruption scandal has metastasized to Stage 4 and will kill him soon; society is on the verge of revolt thanks to plunging quality of life and the aggressive conscription campaign; and the EU has run out of money to help him.

Zelenskiy has run out of time. He has been touring the world to get more interceptors and money and failed in both endeavours. He has already run out of men. Putin has also just taken his “Pandora’s box” campaign up a level and is now talking about the “total destruction” of Ukraine’s infrastructure. That is manifest by the systematic targeting of substations that cut cities off from the NPPs, the last source of power in the country. Blackouts in some cities are already lasting 22 hours.

But there is a lot more common ground than usual. The big changes include:
- The US offered a real security deal as part of December’s 27-point peace plan (27PPP) and this seems to still be on the table;
- Russia is also being offered a real security deal, which was mentioned before but is now centre stage;
- Having been excluded before, everyone, including the Kremlin, agree that Europe (but not the EU) has to be involved in the deal;
- Everyone agrees that Zelenskiy will have to give up some land (Donbas) and Zelenskiy has signalled that he is willing to think about it – provided his security deal is good enough; (this is the potential dealbreaker).

What this all boils down to is they are discussing a new post-Cold War pan-European security deal – something we have been calling for, for more than a decade. This whole war started because of Putin’s concern (paranoia) over Nato’s expansion to the Ukrainian border and Russia’s de facto exclusion from the European security architecture which designated it a de facto “enemy”. This was Putin’s “Cuban missile crisis” moment, whatever you think about it.

Security deals

Top tier delegates from all sides are at this meeting for what is the most important diplomatic encounter since US President Donald Trump restarted negotiations in Riyadh on February 18, 2025.

The World Health Organisation has warned of a looming humanitarian crisis. Countries like Germany are quietly preparing for a fresh million-strong wave of refugees. Electricity, heating, water supplies and essential healthcare, are all being targeted, even schools, potentially leaving millions of Ukrainians without any basic services during the coldest part of the year. This was all entirely predictable, but despite Zelenskiy best efforts he has been unable to avoid the looming missile barrage.

The disaster to come has focused everyone on more realistic goals. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made that change explicit on November 9, saying out loud that, “any security guarantees for Ukraine must also be acceptable to Moscow,” which is new.

"Those security guarantees are going to be key in order for Ukraine to be able to agree to something. But it has to be something Russia agrees to as well," Rubio told reporters.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who is usually scathing about any talk of peace deals, immediately welcomed the shift.

"The very agenda of the talks in Abu Dhabi assumes the first item on the security of Russia, Ukraine and, in general, security in this region. We only welcome such an approach," Lavrov said on November 9, which is also new.

This is a big shift as security deals were built into the heart of the failed 2022 Istanbul peace deal, but Zelenskiy rejected that after he was told by former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson that the West were not prepared to back those deals and to “fight on”, according to reports. In the first year of the war Ukraine’s western allies believed the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) was in with a fighting chance to stave off the Russian invasion; the news of the devastation since Ukraine launched Operation Wildberries in July now make it clear Ukraine’s very survival as a functioning country is on the line.

It has been the running out of air defence ammo that has been the game changer. Under the latest deal, Kyiv gets 12 interceptors a month; it can fire one rocket every three days. Russia has stockpiled some 700 ballistic missiles and makes 50 new ones a day (plus it gets extras from North Korea). German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said yesterday that Germany has no more rockets to give Ukraine until 2027; Portugal will send a package, but only in 2028; and Trump’s deal to sell Ukraine 500 won’t kick in until the middle of 2030 – three years from now. Ukraine needs at least 350 fresh interceptor missiles today.

Zelenskiy has been toughing it out until now, counting on more support from allies, but the rug has been pulled from under his feet now and with winter only a month away he has to face up to the realities of his situation.

The elephant in the room: iron-clad guarantees

The question of Russia's relationship with Nato has been at the heart of Moscow's objections to the post-Cold War European order for more than two decades. Nato began expanding eastwards in 1999, when Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic joined the alliance. Further rounds of enlargement brought Nato closer to Russia's borders, culminating in Finland's accession in 2023 and Sweden's in 2024.

Putin has consistently presented that expansion, and particularly the possibility of Ukraine joining Nato, as a threat to Russian security and one of the principal justifications for the invasion.

That explanation is strongly contested in the West, but it looks like both Europe and Bankova are finally going to have address the “elephant in the room,” as analyst Julie Wilhelmsen, a professor at the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI), recently dubbed it. Rhetoric is suddenly giving way to realpolitik.

The shift to facing the Nato security issues is highlighted by Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov's sudden reappearance in the proceedings. Vladimir Medinsky, the Kremlin aide who did the Istanbul deal, leads the delegation again – and this makes it clear the Kremlin want a new deal on those same lines – but Ryabkov is the one that lead the first attempt to get legally “iron-clad guarantees” that Ukraine would never join Nato in talks with then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in the Geneva talks in January 2022. He said “no” and the war started a month later.

The idea that Russia will insist on its own “ironclad” security guarantees as part of any ceasefire deal has been kicking around for a while; Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko who is also on the Russian team said so in March 2025.

In a tell of how much closer the two sides have moved is Zelenskiy has also suddenly started talking about “iron-clad guarantees" for Ukraine in the last week for the first time.

Donbas

The other half of the equation is Zelenskiy will have to give up the Donbas. This is non-negotiable for the Kremlin. And everyone on the Western side, apart from Zelenskiy, seems to have already concede it: Kushner said earlier this month that if Zelenskiy agrees “the deal is done”; Finnish President Alexander Stubb also said territory will have to be conceded following his talk with Putin.

"I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's gonna happen and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine," Trump said in an interview with CBS's 60 Minutes broadcast on November 8.

US negotiators believe a possible compromise could combine territorial arrangements with an end to the fighting, security guarantees and a roadmap towards Ukrainian membership of the European Union, almost all of which was in the deal thrashed out at the Moscow meeting on December 3 between the US envoys and Putin.

What is new is Zelenskiy hinted that he was open to discussing the question of territory ahead to the Abu Dhabi talks. In fact, he has long realised that he could lose Donbas; in a little remembered story, Zelenskiy previously raised the possibility of a referendum on territorial concessions in August 2024 as ceding sovereign land is barred by the Constitution. Needless to say that it’s a highly unpopular idea, but the increasingly weary population conceded that it would accept losing some land in exchange for the “fair peace,” according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll earlier this year.

Zelenskiy problem is that giving up Donbas is to give up the bulwark of the so-called Fortress cities that holds off Russian troops from walking cross the rest of lightly defended eastern Ukraine right up to the Dnipro River that cuts the country in two. If he concedes the region then the security guarantee has to be strong enough that Russia cannot invade for a second time to take half the country on a whim, up from the 20% it now holds, without sparking WWIII. If he gets less than this he will not do the deal.

What next?

The meetings are unlikely to produce much comment other than the usual “productive progress” talk as they are not about cutting a deal today. There could be the usual POW swap agreement to give the delegates something concrete to say.

The talks are also unlike to float the idea of going back the European security deal that then President Dmitri Medvedev offered to Europe on taking office in 2008 that is still on the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, that ironically would have prevented the Ukraine war from starting in the first place. Another piece of common ground that could be used to push the talks along is to restart all the Cold War-era missile agreements that Putin has made it clear he wants to revive and that Trump initially was also keen on.

The goals in these talks is to map out the ground. It will be followed by a trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month where Beijing is likely to try and push the negotiations forward as despite backing Russia, the Chinese are unhappy with the chaos the war is causing. And Stubb made it clear the goal in this process is to try and prepare the ground for a head-to-head meeting between Putin and Zelenskiy, which is where the really big deal on territory will be done.

In the Istanbul deal it was agreed that Kyiv would agree status of the Crimea would remain undecided for 30 years and under de facto Russian control, but not de jura. Also the status of the four regions annexed by Russia would also be left to be resolved at a face-to-face meeting between Zelenskiy and Putin. A similar proposal is very likely on the cards again, especially with Medinsky leading the Russian side who cut that deal before.

The rest is details. Where the line of contact will be frozen is a tricky one and as IntelliNewsreported the doves in the Kremlin want to freeze it at the current line of contact whereas the hawks want a general mobilisation and flood Donbas with troops to win a quick end to the war. Limits on size of the AFU will also be an issue, as will if Russia gets a veto over any security deals for Ukraine. But the choices are stark. In the best case scenario Ukraine will get some sort of Finlandisation deal, return to neutrality and retain its sovereignty. In the worst case it will end up like Afghanistan, a failed state with its economy in tatters.

Kevin Hart was offered a piece of Uber for $50,000 to $75,000. He said no because it sounded "like Murderville."

Mark Cuban passed on it too, and he knew the founder.

Hart, on the pitch from Troy Carter:

"There's an app, and you say you need a ride, and one of the drivers under our app will come get you."

"I was like, 'Sounds like Murderville to me.'"

"I said, 'You ask me to pick somebody up. I don't know that person. I ain't picking them up.'"

Cuban had already saved Travis Kalanick's first company when it was running out of money:

"He comes to me, like, 'I got this thing. It's gonna replace taxicab.' It was called UberCab at the time. I still got the emails."

"I'm like, 'I love it, I love it.' But he had a valuation of like $10 million, and I said, 'I'll do it at $5 million valuation.' Never came back to me."

Hart's math on what he missed:

"If I would've given him 250 grand on a $5 million or $10 million valuation, it'd be billions."

Uber went public at an $82 billion valuation.

Moving forward after the Midterm elections of 2026, the Strategy and policies towards the Middle East that are recommended:

The Middle East (Thanassis Cambanis and Zaha Hassan)
 It is no secret that the United States has a Middle East problem. For decades, US leaders have made deals with dictators in the mistaken belief that friendly authoritarian regimes could ensure American regional interests. Stability mattered to the United States to enable the uninterrupted flow of oil and other petrochemicals from the region. Well-armed autocrats, US policymakers believed, provided the best guarantee. In fact, the opposite is true. Under these misguided assumptions, Washington has become one of the main drivers of regional conflict, from the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 to the joint US-Israeli war on Iran in 2026. This has been catastrophic for millions across the Middle East and North Africa, with toxic blowback for the United States as well. True safety and stability require respect for rights, good governance, and freedom from fear and violence. For too long, US leaders have deemed otherwise for the Middle East, settling instead for short-term authoritarian bargains. Local autocrats win US military backing in exchange for limited asks that only deepen instability: weapons deals, new bases, oil-market cooperation, support for Israel, or assistance in another military campaign or political crackdown. 54THE MiDDLE EAST The US relationship with Israel represents the most pernicious example of that logic. For decades, the US government has professed support for a two-state solution while helping Israel make a Palestinian state impossible. Along the way Washington has been complicit in Israeli war crimes and joined in reckless wars that have made the Middle East the world’s most dangerous and unstable region. Today, Washington’s special relationship with Israel is best understood as an alliance with an expansionist, authoritarian state that falsely bills itself as the “only democracy in the Middle East” while making common cause with the United States to violently extend illiberal, ethnonationalist policies to millions of Arab subjects and neighbors. There is a better way. US policy in the Middle East has been so bad for so long that a new US administration has ample room to repair harm and promote the common good. The starting point: there is no stability without justice and accountable governance. The United States cannot, and need not, be in the business of dictating terms to or fixing Middle Eastern governments; nor should we abruptly disengage from the region. We cannot impose global order or energy security by bombing foreign nations. Military force does not solve political problems. The 2026 US-Israeli war on Iran is a case in point. Trump’s wars with Tehran in 2025 and 2026 illustrate the limits of force along with the need for diplomacy. The United States should not ignore Iran’s nuclear program and support for hybrid and proxy militias in other countries, but a war without even consultation with those in the region who would be most affected was not the answer. Trump realized every American war hawk’s dreams by joining Israel to attack Iran, but the US bombings in June 2025 emboldened the Iranian government while failing to end its nuclear program. The catastrophic US-Israeli war launched in February 2026 produced a far more radical, centralized and militarized Iranian leadership, which immediately, and predictably, exercised its own leverage in response to the American resort to force. Iran now determines whether roughly 55A WORLD FOR ALL one-fourth of the world’s energy supplies can reach markets through the Strait of Hormuz. Brute force produced not clarity and security, but instead introduced chaotic uncertainty to world markets, and strengthened the most radical strains in the Iranian state. Only sustained diplomacy, peacemaking, and political compromise can reverse the harm. The question is how we engage. The United States can stop providing aid and cover to Arab regimes that abuse their citizens, and enabling an Israeli government addicted to repression and war. We should use the full range of our policy tools—military assistance, political support, and economic investment—to promote regional peace and economic integration conditioned on respect for internationally recognized borders. A US policy that promotes peace and justice in the Middle East will end the United States’s direct complicity in rights violations and reduce the torrent of armed conflict and abuse of power. Economic and political engagement must replace our habitual reflex to address every concern with military force. Over time, this will encourage peace and good governance in a region craving stability to meet development challenges and take advantage of its natural resources and human capital. We can begin a new era of US foreign policy starting in the Middle East—the same region where the United States forged a decades-long record of war and lawlessness that diminished and destabilized both. To begin recalibrating its policy, the United States will have to conclusively end its war with Iran and the related regional conflicts that have flared since October 2023; responsibly wind down forever wars; promote a just peace between Palestinians and Israelis; end support for the military campaigns and occupations conducted by US allies; and finally, ensure that US military aid complies with federal statutes and international law. This approach stands the best chance of creating the conditions for sustainable development, safety, and prosperity for all. 56THE MiDDLE EAST Generation war Even before but especially following 9/11, the United States has tried to impose security and stability on the Middle East through violence. Washington abandoned its professed values and policy interests in pursuit of a single, poorly defined counterterrorism agenda. This produced the forever wars that the United States is still fighting today, which have, predictably, provided an ongoing recruitment boon to the heirs of Al Qaeda. Perpetual war and military occupation in the Middle East have wreaked havoc on the region and its people, savaged the rule of law, undermined America’s global standing, siphoned taxpayer funds away from much needed domestic programs, left nearly a million US veterans seriously injured, negatively impacted American civil liberties, and brought political violence to the home front. When each new round of warfare fails to produce its promised results, the hawks invoke the magical thinking of “more force,” promising that if only the United States with its regional ally, Israel, apply enough of it, they can achieve total victory. This faulty logic reached its apotheosis with the reckless and ill-fated war against Iran in February 2026. Most presidents since 9/11 have paid only lip service to ideals of democracy and accountable governance. George W. Bush touted a “freedom agenda” even as he led the invasion and occupation of Afghanistan and Iraq. Barack Obama praised the popular Arab uprisings against repressive rule but ended up super-charging military partnerships with Arab authoritarians fueling wars in Yemen, Libya, and Syria. Joe Biden campaigned on a promise to put democratic values at the center of America’s alliance structure but quickly dropped his criticism of human rights abuses by Saudi Arabia and others in pursuit of military partnerships, expansion of Trump’s Abraham Accords, and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Donald Trump, on the other hand, dispensed with even the pretense of humanitarian values, courting Saudi investment and praising Egypt’s authoritarian leader as “my favorite dictator.”  57A WORLD FOR ALL In his second term, he promised to restore US global dominance by force while undermining the UN and other multilateral institutions. Over the last quarter-century, the core US policies have remained remarkably and distressingly consistent, refracted through the distorted prism of the “War on Terror.” The Middle East is the United States’s main market for weapons. Across a sprawling network of bases, detention centers, and paramilitary partnerships, US authorities have mastered a host of undesirable skills, including rendition, torture, and warzone cronyism. Nowhere was US transactionalism more vivid and destructive than in Israel and occupied Palestine, where US policy enabled extremist Israeli policies, increased settlements and land grabs, and produced endless conflict culminating in ongoing mass atrocities, crimes in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. US support for genocide in Gaza accelerated the moral hazard of total war extremists and grew into a delusional and destructive joint US-Israeli campaign against Iran. The United States squandered its influence to cultivate alliances with Middle Eastern governments that prioritize regime survival over the well-being of their citizens. These regimes have recklessly pursued a flurry of wars and wantonly repressed their subjects, all while receiving weapons, intelligence, political cover, and often financial assistance from Washington, while showing little interest in genuinely delivering the security and stability that American support is purportedly buying. Farewell to arms, hello diplomacy The United States should dramatically reduce its military footprint in the Middle East and discourage unreliable partners and allies from starting wars they believe the United States will finish for them. Instead, the United States should implement a less militarized, more consistent arms-length approach to the region. These broad principles translate 58THE MiDDLE EAST into Middle East policies that draw the United States out of conflicts— including conflicts that are likely to continue even without a US role— while keeping the United States invested in diplomacy. The United States cannot create a demilitarized Middle East, but it can leverage American influence in support of a nuclear-free region and encourage a regional security architecture that enables diplomacy and conflict resolution. Middle Eastern states won’t accept the lopsided status quo, in which a nuclear-armed Israel supercharged with a US-backed qualitative military edge inflicts perpetual wars on its neighbors. Iran’s commitment to its nuclear program stems in part from this structural imbalance. Either the United States pushes for a truly nuclear-free Middle East, or else it accepts that regional powers (and not just Iran) will seek the deterrent power that only weapons of mass destruction can provide. The United States must finally recalibrate security assistance to the region to ensure that it comports with federal laws that prohibit weapons transfers to states that consistently violate human rights or who use those weapons for non-defensive purposes. The United States should begin to wean itself from blockbuster weapons deals and long-term security agreements that create domestic dependencies and bind the United States from being able to withhold transfers when such action is required. In place of permissive weapons transfers, Washington should use diplomacy and regional alliance networks to provide assurances to Arab states in the Gulf who have spent considerable money on US defense contracts and have legitimate security concerns. Washington’s industrial policy should protect the defense industry’s high-quality jobs by redirecting them to other manufacturing needs, including green energy. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), the Middle East stands as the primary destination for US weapons exports and the United States serves as the region’s dominant weapons provider. The United States supplies 52 percent of all arms in the Middle East, followed by France at a mere 12 percent.1 59A WORLD FOR ALL US military assistance to the Middle East has outpaced economic aid by a staggering factor of roughly thirty to one, reflecting our distorted priorities. In the first two years since October 7, 2023, the United States spent more than $30 billion on Israel’s conflicts alone. This assistance enabled an ongoing Israeli military campaign that has so far killed or wounded at least 10 percent of Gaza’s population.2 Meanwhile, US diplomats pressured Arab Gulf countries to normalize relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords despite overwhelming domestic opposition to any engagement with Israel.3 All that misplaced policy attention resolved none of the Middle East’s conflicts. A less militarized Middle East policy would create a pathway for the United States to contain the spread of violence from Gaza to the wider region, instead of what the United States has actually done since October 7: to participate directly in Israel’s war with Yemen’s Houthis, militias in Iraq, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Iran itself. Of course, even if the United States staunches the flood of weapons to the region, regional belligerents can still shop for guns and ammunition elsewhere, but a better US policy and diplomatic engagement can shift momentum away from war. At the very least, it can end direct US complicity in war crimes and rights violations, a worthy goal in and of itself. Fewer bases, less moral hazard The US military must substantially lighten its footprint in the Central Command areas of operations, covering most Middle East hotspots. Sprawling bases that have effectively become permanent should be replaced with bilateral agreements that allow the United States to deploy forces to national facilities during emergencies. Maintaining tens of thousands of troops in Iraq, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain, along with bombers and naval craft, is no longer sustainable, particularly given affordability concerns domestically. (The precipitous US withdrawal from Northeast Syria underscores the 60THE MiDDLE EAST problems with an overextended US military footprint.) Nor should Israel continue to enjoy a blank check when it comes to its reliance on the United States for military support, especially when this involves violating federal and international law and ignoring US advice. This posture only creates expectations among other US allies who will want the United States to back them up and bail them out when they resort to war that goes beyond their control. To be sure, leaders in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar have complained at various points that the United States has not adequately helped them when attacked; some governments have gone so far as to diversify weapons suppliers. But all depend overwhelmingly on US security guarantees and the interoperability of US weapons systems. Despite declarations of disappointment, they will continue to turn to the United States for the foreseeable future. But there is also a moral hazard for Washington. US Air Force and Navy assets deployed to the Middle East tend not to idle long, or, in the case of the deployments in Syria and Iraq, are prone to attack by local militias. The result has been a constantly deepening US involvement in conflicts of only marginal importance to the national interest. The United States should move quickly to end all ongoing military interventions and reduce remaining military deployments in the region. Missions in conflict zones such as Iraq should be reduced to the barest minimum: small, internationalized missions that focus on law enforcement training consistent with internationally recognized standards and best practices and legitimate counterterrorism activities. Faced with the collapse of Washington’s Syrian Kurdish partners, Trump withdrew a US mission in Syria that should have ended years earlier. In the Gulf, the president, working with Congress, should create a time-bound commission to streamline  deployments and defense commitments, with the goal of replacing permanent deployments with over-the-horizon capabilities. A reassessment is also necessary, albeit more complicated, with Jordan, Egypt, and Israel, where security 61A WORLD FOR ALL commitments are considered a cornerstone of peace agreements. By now, however, it’s clear that the peace treaties between Israel and Egypt and Jordan don’t depend on continued US military aid; they reflect the perceived national interests of the signatories. The United States will have to make some painful decisions as it untangles the knots of its forever wars. The sudden end of the Syria mission illustrates the risks of extending deployments too long, refusing to negotiate an exit, and then leaving because of conflict. The United States stationed troops in Syria for a decade and passed up multiple opportunities to negotiate an exit that would have secured the tens of thousands of Islamic State detainees held in the northeastern part of the country—a legitimate international security interest. While the new Syrian leadership under Ahmed Al-Sharaa regained control of the Kurdish autonomous zone, the United States failed to support arrangements for a responsible transition. Overnight, the United States had to evacuate dangerous Islamic State detainees to Iraqi prisons—once again postponing a reckoning that must involve due process for the thousands of prisoners in indefinite detention. A responsible resolution for the ISIS detainees should set the standard for accountability and rule of law. National courts or a regional commission should review their cases, offer reparations where appropriate, and restore citizenship to all those wrongfully stripped of their status. Transitional justice for ISIS detainees requires the application of international law and due process and an end to the widespread practice of prolonged extrajudicial detention. Respect for the laws of war and humanitarian principles must be restored. The United States’s alliances with Saudi Arabia and Israel have emboldened those leaders to launch reckless, unwinnable wars with high civilian casualties—as was illustrated with the Saudi war on Yemen and Israel’s military campaigns to destroy civilian infrastructure and forcibly displace populations in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and beyond. While a reset might not curtail the bad behavior of regional leaders, it will certainly lessen US culpability, begin to restore US credibility, 62THE MiDDLE EAST and better enable the United States to effectively support conflict- resolution efforts. Dignity and rights for both Palestinians and Israelis For many Americans—and for much of the world—unconditional support for Israel has come to exemplify American hypocrisy. While both Democrat and Republican administrations have professed support for international law and human rights in the conduct of foreign policy, all too often the United States has provided aid to and political cover for those engaged in gross violations of those norms. The United States has neither been true to American values nor its stated policy objectives when it comes to Palestine-Israel. Likewise, many self-identified progressives have earned the derisive label of “progressive except for Palestine” for their unconditional support to Israel even as it committed grave human rights abuses and imposed a regime of apartheid over Palestinians. This dissonance has impacted how Americans view Israel and continued US support to the country.4 A growing percentage of Americans wants to end unconditional support for Israel’s military adventurism and its denial of Palestinian rights.5 Polls show that Americans today want a United States that is “engaged but not entangled,” “principled but modest.”6 And as the hundreds of thousands of protestors across the United States made clear following the launch of Israel’s war on Gaza in 2023, Americans want to see a US policy that supports a just peace in occupied Palestine, where the United States has provided billions in aid and dedicated an outsized amount of policy attention, and where it has played such a central role in perpetuating the daily violence of military occupation. It is no longer plausible to pretend that the Middle East can achieve regional stability without a just peace between Palestinians and Israelis. In a binding legal determination, the International Court of Justice 63A WORLD FOR ALL ruled a plausible case has been made that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza,7 and in a separate advisory opinion, found Israel’s prolonged occupation of Palestine illegal and its regime over Palestinians one of apartheid.8 With International Criminal Court arrest warrants out for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes including use of starvation as a weapon of war, and a UN International Commission of Inquiry and the world’s largest professional association of genocide scholars finding Israel’s actions in Gaza genocide, the United States can no longer turn a blind eye and maintain a “no daylight” approach between the two countries.9 Because of the failure of the United States to act to restrain Israel as it launched a war on the civilian population in Gaza, the violence expanded to additional fronts across the Middle East, including Iran, Yemen, Syria, and Lebanon. Worse still, the United States joined directly in strikes on Iran and Yemen and provided the bulk of the munitions for the rest of Israel’s ongoing wars. And America’s participation in the Gaza genocide by continuing to arm Israel, and in attacking Iran in 2025, has emboldened Israel to move ground forces into Lebanon to seize territory and depopulate vast stretches of the South. According to Israeli political and military leaders, the aim is permanent displacement and the creation of uninhabited buffer zones, in violation of international law. In addition, the United States has provided political support and diplomatic cover for Israeli war crimes in international fora, heightening already serious legal concerns about American complicity in occupation, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The United States should swiftly stop these abuses by halting weapons shipments to Israel, condition bilateral relations on Israel reversing its expansionist campaigns of depopulation, ethnic cleansing and settlement expansion, and ceasing use of the US veto power to shield Israel from opprobrium at the UN. 64THE MiDDLE EAST A just peace is not an abstraction; it will determine whether a child in Gaza will have a future or whether she will die under a brutal blockade and a deliberate policy of deprivation. It will also determine whether families in Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and the rest of the Middle East can live in safety and equal dignity. Serious investment will be required in reaching a political solution between Palestinians and Israelis. It starts with a United States that conclusively abandons its role as defender of Israeli occupation and uses its influence with Israel to compel it to abide by international law and live in peace and security alongside Palestinians who enjoy the same rights and responsibilities. Only respect for fundamental rights and freedoms, justice, and a commitment to the rule of law will bring an end to war—and only equal rights and good governance can create stability and a durable peace. To promote cooperation instead of war, the United States will have to do what it supposedly has asked of Middle Eastern countries—it must normalize its relationship with Israel. In Washington’s case, normalization would entail treating Israel like any other state, and not as a special case exempt from international norms. A better US approach would end blank-check military support for Israel. The United States, which enabled the destruction of Gaza and the creeping annexation of the West Bank, should invest in Palestinian communities and in Palestinian-led rehabilitation and reconstruction. Security assistance and economic aid to Israelis and Palestinians should be premised on a new order that requires respect for international law. Israelis and Palestinians will have to decide for themselves whether to live in two separate sovereign states, a single binational state with equal rights for all citizens, or a confederation—but the United States should only support a solution that enables Palestinians and Israelis to enjoy the same rights and freedoms in safety and security. Restorative justice and reparation will be critical to the durability of any peace agreement between the parties. 65A WORLD FOR ALL Our historic relationship to Israel means that the United States bears responsibility to course correct now.

How to read bonus terms before you claim anything 🧐

A "200% welcome bonus" sounds better than a 50% one. Often it isn't.

What a bonus is really worth sits in the terms and conditions, which most players skip. UK bonus rules changed a lot in 2026, so here's how to read the terms properly, and what's now allowed for UK players.

1️⃣ Wagering requirements: the number that matters most

The wagering requirement (also called the playthrough or rollover) is how many times you have to bet the bonus before you can withdraw it, or anything you win with it.

📌 The UK rule: since January 2026, UKGC-licensed casinos can't set wagering above 10x. Offers of 35x or 50x used to be common, but a licensed UK site can no longer use them.
Example:
• You deposit £100 and get a 100% match, so a £100 bonus
• The wagering is 10x
• You have to place £1,000 in total bets before you can cash out
Why the cap makes a big difference:
Every bet has a house edge. On a slot with 96% RTP, the long-run average loss is about 4% of what you wager.
• Old style: £100 × 35x = £3,500 wagered, and 4% of that is about £140 expected loss. That's more than the bonus.
• Now: £100 × 10x = £1,000 wagered, and 4% of that is about £40 expected loss. That leaves £60 of value on average.
Results in a single session can be very different from these averages, but the trend is clear: lower wagering means a better bonus.

💡 Compare within the cap. 10x is the maximum, not the standard. 5x is better than 10x, and wager-free (0x) is the most transparent of all.

🚩 If you see 35x or 50x on a UK-facing site, treat it as a warning sign. It suggests the site isn't UKGC licensed, so UK player protections don't apply. Check the licence (see section 9).

2️⃣ Game weighting: not every bet counts the same
Most casinos count different games towards wagering at different rates. A common setup:
• Slots: 100%
• Scratchcards / instant games: 100% or 50%
• Roulette: 10–20%
• Blackjack: 5–10%
• Live casino: 0–10%
• Some slots: 0% (excluded completely)
If blackjack counts at 10%, a £10 hand only clears £1 of your wagering. Clearing even £1,000 would take £10,000 of blackjack bets.
Check for two things:
• The weighting table, which is usually in the bonus terms or a separate "bonus policy" page
• The excluded games list. High-RTP slots and jackpot games are often on it. Play an excluded game with bonus funds and you could lose your winnings.

📌 Since January 2026, UK operators also can't run "mixed-product" promotions that require you to use, say, both the casino and the sportsbook to unlock a bonus. A casino bonus should only need casino play.

3️⃣ Maximum bet while the bonus is active 🚫
This rule catches more players than any other.
Most bonuses limit how much you can bet per spin or hand while bonus funds are active. Go over it, even once and even by accident, and the casino can cancel the bonus and any winnings from it.

📌 There are two limits to keep in mind in the UK:
• The legal slot stake limit: £5 per spin if you're 25 or over, £2 per spin if you're 18–24. This applies to all online slots play, with or without a bonus.
• The bonus max bet: a casino's own limit while you're wagering, which can be lower than the legal limit. £1–£2 per spin is common.
What to check:
• The exact limit in the bonus terms
• Whether it's per spin, per hand or per round
• Whether bonus-buy features or double-up/gamble features count as breaking it (they often do)

4️⃣ Maximum cashout: the ceiling on your winnings
Some bonuses cap how much you can withdraw from bonus play, no matter how much you win.
Example:
• You claim 50 free spins
• You hit a big win of £800
• The terms say "max cashout £100"
• You can withdraw £100 and the other £700 is removed
Caps are most common on:
• No-deposit bonuses
• Free spins offers
• Reload and loyalty promos
A capped bonus isn't automatically bad, but you should know about the cap before you start playing. UKGC rules say significant terms like this must be clear and shown next to the offer, so if it's hidden, that's a bad sign.

5️⃣ Time limits ⏳
Bonuses expire, and usually there are two clocks:
• Time to claim or activate: often 24 hours to 7 days after you sign up or deposit
• Time to complete wagering: commonly 7–30 days
Even at 10x, a short deadline can push you to play more than you planned. £1,000 of wagering in 3 days is over £330 a day. If the deadline feels tight, you can skip the bonus.
Free spins often have their own expiry, sometimes just 24 hours after they're credited.

6️⃣ Which deposits and payment methods qualify
Before you deposit, check:
• The minimum deposit. Deposit £9 when the minimum is £10 and you may get no bonus.
• Excluded payment methods. E-wallets such as PayPal, Skrill and Neteller are sometimes excluded from welcome offers.
• Bonus codes. Some offers need a code at the cashier. Forget it and you usually can't add the bonus afterwards.
• Opt-in. UK bonuses have to be opt-in, so look for the tick box or "claim" button before you deposit.

📌 Credit cards have been banned for gambling in the UK since 2020, so the usual options are debit card, e-wallet, open banking or bank transfer.

7️⃣ How your money and the bonus money interact 🔄
This is less obvious but important. When you have both real money and bonus money, the casino needs a rule for which one you're betting with.
Real money first
This is standard at most UK casinos. Your deposit is used first, and it stays yours to withdraw at any time, even while a bonus is active.
Bonus funds kept separate
Bonus money, and winnings from it, stay locked until wagering is complete. If you withdraw early, you normally lose only the bonus part.
UK regulators have taken action against casinos that blocked players from withdrawing their own deposit because of a bonus. If a site's terms say your real money is locked until you finish wagering, read them carefully and think twice.
Also check whether you can cancel a bonus. A good casino lets you forfeit it and keep your real-money balance.

8️⃣ Free spins have their own rules 🎰
Free spins seem simple, but check:
• Spin value. "100 free spins" at 10p each is £10 of play. 20 spins at £1 each is £20. Compare the total value, not the number of spins.
• Eligible game. Usually one specific slot.
• Wagering on winnings. Look for "no wagering" free spins, where winnings are paid as cash. They're common in the UK and usually the best option.
• Max cashout. Covered above, and very common on spins.
• How they're released. "100 spins" might arrive as 10 a day for 10 days, and you may have to log in daily to collect them.

9️⃣ Check the license first 🚩
All the protections above only apply if the casino holds a UK Gambling Commission license.
How to check:
• Scroll to the footer of the casino's site and find the UKGC license number
• Look the number up in the public register on the Gambling Commission's website
• Make sure the company name matches the site
Be careful if you see:
• No UKGC license, or only an offshore license on a site aimed at UK players
• Wagering above 10x
• "Not on GAMSTOP" used as a selling point
• Vague terms like "irregular play" that are never defined
• Key terms that are hidden or only appear in a separate document
Unlicensed sites aren't bound by UK rules on wagering, stake limits, fair terms or self-exclusion, and you'd have little recourse if a withdrawal went wrong.

✅ The 60-second checklist before you claim
1. Is the casino UKGC licensed?
2. What's the wagering? It can't be above 10x, but lower is better.
3. How much do my preferred games count?
4. What's the bonus max bet per spin or hand?
5. Is there a max cashout?
6. How long do I have?
7. Does my payment method qualify, and do I need to opt in or use a code?
8. Can I withdraw my own deposit at any time?
If you can't find an answer to any of these, ask live chat before you deposit and screenshot the reply.

$UEIC Q3 2026 earnings: Universal Electronics kept sales steady, but its parts cost more

Universal Electronics, which makes remote controls and thermostats that other brands sell, held its sales steady and earned more. Sales of $89.4 million landed within about 1% of a year earlier, after a far deeper drop in the spring. Costs came down faster than sales, so profit per share excluding one-offs doubled. Chief executive Wade Jenke left the full-year plan unchanged, which by our math leaves a smaller fourth quarter than last year's.

• Sales: $𝟖𝟗.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (−1% from a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟏𝟕 ($0.08 a year ago)
• Gross margin, excluding one-offs: 𝟐𝟔.𝟑% (29.1% a year ago)
• Full-year profit outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 ($0.45–$0.65 a share, with $0.42 earned in nine months)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The standing case got better, because the yearly profit target the company set now looks reachable. Through nine months it has earned $0.42 of a plan that asks for at least $0.45 a share, and climate-control sales grew again after a long slide. One caution: the cost of making its products rose, so gross margin narrowed even as overheads came down. The improvement came from running the company more cheaply, not from making things more cheaply.

The question now is whether earnings can keep climbing once the savings are spent. Jenke said surcharges and permanent price rises recover about three-quarters of the inflation the company has identified, but most of that money only starts arriving in the first quarter of 2027. If customers accept the new prices, gross margin recovers and the thin profit holds; if they refuse, overheads must carry everything again. The fourth-quarter gross margin will show which way it goes.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐨𝐧 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Universal Electronics has spent a year taking out the cost of running itself rather than waiting for demand to recover. The release says "we significantly reduced our operational costs" in the quarter, and finance chief Raymond Ho put the fall in operating expenses excluding one-offs at a fifth.

• Operating expenses excluding one-offs: $19.9 million, $4.9 million below last year
• Share of sales they take: 22.2%, against 27.3%
• Research and development: 4.8% of sales, from 7.4%
• Selling, general and administrative costs: 18.4% of sales, from 24.4%
• Profit per share excluding one-offs: $0.17, against $0.08

Those savings reached earnings because sales barely moved, so nothing had to be spent to win them. Operating profit excluding one-offs came to $3.7 million against $1.6 million, and Ho described the result as "reflecting continued progress in aligning our cost structure with current revenue levels". Actions taken in August and October add about $2.5 million of yearly savings on top.

What to watch: operating expenses in the fourth quarter, when freight and volume costs usually rise. If they stay near $20 million, the yearly profit target holds without any help from the factory, and the cost base becomes the reason to own the shares rather than a one-quarter effect.

🟢 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐇𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐔𝐩
Connected home is the part of Universal Electronics that sells climate controls, smart thermostats and security sensors to manufacturers. Sales there had fallen for four quarters. In this one they reached $33.8 million, nearly 14% above a year ago, which the company puts down to "stronger sales in the HVAC market and increased sales of recently launched thermostat products".

Chief executive Wade Jenke named the programmes behind the turn: a smart thermostat now ramping at a large air-conditioning maker, and with Daikin, "we won the primary wireless remote program for the Asian market". One quarter settles little here, because Daikin alone bought 22% of everything the group sold, so a single order change moves this line either way.

What to watch: connected home sales in the fourth quarter against last year's $29.7 million. A second reading above that level would mark the recovery as a programme ramp rather than one customer restocking after a weak spring.

🟢 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤
Universal Electronics put cash at the top of its release: $41.4 million at the end of September, up $9.1 million this year. The quarter itself brought in $11.1 million from operations. Subtract the credit lines and net cash comes to $21.7 million by our math, nearly twice the level three months earlier.

That shift matters because the group spent two years repaying borrowings while losing money, and nothing is now drawn on its American credit line. The release credits "Continued focus on working capital". The nine-month inflow of $16.6 million still sits below last year's $27.8 million, when collapsing sales released cash from customer balances that will not repeat.

What to watch: operating cash flow in the fourth quarter. Jenke said the company is buying material early for 2027 programmes, so cash can go backwards even while profit holds, and the next reading shows whether this year's build survives that buying.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐛𝐢 𝐇𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Universal Electronics buys chips, circuit boards and capacitors and builds remotes and thermostats in Asia. What it pays for those parts sets its gross margin, the share of sales left after production costs. That share came to 26.3% in the quarter, against 29.1% a year earlier on the same basis, and the filing blames "higher component costs due to market conditions".

• Higher component costs: 4.2 percentage points off gross margin
• A stronger Chinese renminbi: 1.7 points off
• Better sales mix: 1.4 points back
• Lower labour and factory costs after the Mexico closure: 1.7 points back
• Lower tariff rates: 1.4 points back

This cuts against the company's own headline about reducing costs, because the cost of making the products went the other way: cost of sales took 73.7% of revenue against 72.3%. Jenke said "Input costs remain a material drag" and that lead times on boards and capacitors "have extended from weeks to months". His answer is surcharges and permanent price rises that "recover roughly three-quarters of the inflation we have identified", but he added that "the majority will be starting in Q1 of 2027".

What to watch: gross margin in the fourth quarter and again in the first quarter of 2027, when those new prices reach invoices. A reading still near 26% would leave the yearly profit plan resting on overheads alone, with no second lever if the savings run out.

🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐲-𝐓𝐕 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠
Home entertainment is the larger side of the business: remote controls, chips and software sold to pay-television operators, television makers and retailers. Sales there fell to $55.6 million from $60.8 million, and Jenke said "subscription broadcast demand is still in structural decline due to streaming competition". The filing points to "lower demand for subscription broadcasting products, particularly basic remote controls with lower price points and limited or no advanced features".

The fall is gentler than it was, 9% against about a quarter in the spring, helped by better retail sales. Comcast, the biggest customer in this channel, bought $9.9 million, well below last year. New work is arriving: Jenke said the group was picked as "sole source on two operator remote programs scheduled to enter production this quarter", and he called the India-built remote order "an offering that matters more as rising memory costs make set-top box itself harder to sell".

What to watch: home entertainment sales in the fourth quarter against last year's $58.0 million. Another single-digit decline would show the two sole-source programmes replacing the lost basic-remote volume, which is what keeps this channel paying for the company's research.

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞
Universal Electronics earned an operating profit of $2.9 million and still reported a net loss. The gap is tax: a charge of $1.4 million on pre-tax income of a similar size. Over nine months the arithmetic is starker, with $6.1 million of tax against $73,000 of pre-tax income.

The reason is that the American business loses money and earns no credit for those losses. After three years of cumulative losses the company wrote down the value of its US deferred tax assets at the end of 2025, and it says it expects "the U. S. to be in a pre-tax loss position without benefit for the full year 2026, resulting in an elevated effective tax rate". Brazil's deferred tax assets took a further small write-down this quarter.

Jenke told investors: "The plan we are executing is directed at what matters to shareholders: improving profitability, generating cash, and rebuilding financial flexibility". Cash and flexibility arrived; profitability has not reached the bottom line, where nine months show a loss of $6.0 million. A factory closure approved in October will add charges to that figure.

What to watch: the fourth-quarter tax charge, and whether reported earnings turn positive for the first time since 2022. Until the US operation makes money, profit excluding one-offs will keep describing a better company than the one shareholders own.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing worries got no fresh numbers in these materials, and one of them got worse. None changes the quarter's arithmetic, but each is a route by which the recovery stalls, and for each there is a disclosure that would move the argument one way or the other.

• Customer concentration: Daikin took 22.4% of sales, up from 20.5%, and Comcast another 11.1%; the quarterly filing's customer table shows it.
• Design-win pipeline: no value has been published for the connected home pipeline since early 2025, so the next two years of thermostat volume cannot be sized.
• Forward sales: no range for any coming quarter, a practice the company dropped a year ago; the call offered none either.
• Leadership: Jenke ran his first call as chief executive after a year of change in both top jobs, and no successor plan for the roles below him was described.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐳𝐢𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐲 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
The board approved closing the Brazilian factory in October, "as part of the Company’s ongoing efforts to optimize its global manufacturing footprint and cost structure", with the wind-down substantially finished in the first quarter of 2027. Charges will run to $4.2 million to $5.0 million, "primarily consisting of employee severance and other facility closure costs". Mexico's shutdown, completed last year, cost $4.2 million.

𝐀 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬
The board chose a payout over repurchases: "a special, one-time cash dividend payable in an amount equal to $0.24 per share", about $3.1 million, reached shareholders on 15 October. Universal Electronics bought no shares in the first nine months, even though its directors added a million shares to the repurchase authorisation in March.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟎.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Stock is lighter: $70.1 million, 13% below September last year and $7.7 million below the start of this year. Jenke said "The inventory days are down roughly to 95 days from 128 days a year ago". He also said "we expect inventory to build" modestly in the fourth quarter, because the group is committing 2027 material early.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞, 𝐧𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟖𝟑.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money owed to the company reached $83.5 million, $4.2 million above the start of the year, even though nine-month sales fell. Customers are not paying more slowly: 71 days outstanding against 72 a year ago. Much of the rise sits in supplier and interest claims, $13.1 million of the total, rather than in trade bills.

Cash customers paid in advance for cloud software — the only forward order book the group discloses — slipped to $2.95 million from $3.53 million a year ago. New payments of $0.9 million in the quarter came in under the $1.0 million recognised as revenue, so the balance shrank again, though by less than it did a year earlier.

Unchanged. The plan still calls for $0.45 to $0.65 a share excluding one-offs. Nine months have produced $0.42 of that. By our math the fourth quarter then needs $0.03 to $0.23, whose middle sits a quarter below the $0.17 the company just earned. The same range has now stood for four quarters, and the floor needs three cents more.

Cut. The estimate for equipment and patents is $1.0 million to $1.5 million for the fourth quarter. In August the plan covering the whole half was $3.0 million to $4.0 million. About $1.5 million went out in the third quarter, so by our math the half lands near its lower edge. Fewer plants need less equipment: Mexico has gone and Brazil follows.
