Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks : https://t.co/yMq8SZjfiW

"https://t.co/uSRUKgbPwH  2212-8271 © 2026 The Authors. Published by ELSEVIER B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (https://t.co/SgkcOfXMlR) Peer-review under responsibility of the scientific committee of the 20th CIRP Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering, 8-10 July, Gulf of Naples, Italy 20th CIRP Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks Tim Schniedersa*, Tareq Maximilian Gabriel Ahraria , Oliver Petrovica , Christian Brechera aLaboratory for Machine Tools and Production Engineering (WZL) RWTH Aachen University, Campus-Boulevard 30, 52074 Aachen, Germany * Corresponding author. Tel.: +49-241-8025434. E-mail address: t.schnieders@wzl.rwth-aachen.de Abstract The push towards circularity and Re-X principles presents a challenge to SMEs, particularly due to increasing product complexity that impedes the adoption of disassembly automation. This paper introduces and compares two frameworks for extracting disassembly instructions from unstructured information sources, such as disassembly manuals. Our goal is to transform natural language text into a structured, curated and machine-readable format. We implemented and tested a rule-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework against a generative AI framework leveraging LLMs. The performance of both approaches was compared using real-world disassembly manuals. This work provides the necessary data foundation for developing and automating future disassembly processes. © 2026 The Authors. Accepted Manuscript. Accepted for publication in Procedia CIRP. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (https://t.co/SgkcOfXMlR) Peer-review under responsibility of the scientific committee of the 19th CIRP Conference on Intelligent Computation in Manufacturing Engineering, 8-10 July, Gulf of Naples, Italy Keywords: Natrual Langauage Processing (NLP); Generative Artificial Intelligence, Disassembly, Information extraction; Disassembly manual; Re-X Strategies (Recycling, Repair, Refurbish, Remanufacture); Automated Knowledge Acquisition; Disassembly Sequence Planning (DSP), Large Language Model (LLM); Digital Product Passport (DPP) 1. Introduction The global transition toward a circular economy aims to replace the traditional linear "take-make-dispose" model by extending product lifecycles through Re-X processes, such as repairing, refurbishing, remanufacturing, and recycling [1–3]. While large companies can support circular technology development through internal research and development, Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) often do not have the financial capacity to manage the disruptive transition to a circular business model and must depend on the availability of market technologies [4]. Furthermore, automated disassembly systems only act economically when processing large quantities of products, combined with the high upfront costs and time required for planning reverse logistics, this poses a significant barrier to the adoption of advanced disassembly automation for SMEs [2, 4]. One key enabler for a smart and digitally enabled circular economy is the implementation of the Digital Product Passport (DPP), which aims to provide consistent "track and trace" information on a product's origin, composition, and dismantling options [1, 5]. The DPP acts as a repository for diverse data categories, including guidelines and manuals for non-destructive disassembly [1]. However, the availability and accessibility of data for modeling remains a significant challenge, particularly for SMEs, creating a gap between theoretical DPP concepts and systems that can be readily used [6]. Current disassembly sequence planning still necessitates extensive manual effort, as operators must often search through available online documentation or rely on manually 2 Tim Schnieders et. al./ Procedia CIRP 00 (2026) 000–000 analyzing CAD models to infer priority relationships and disassembly steps [3]. To fully support Re-X ambitions and facilitate automated disassembly, there is a critical need for uniform data structures and automated data extraction methods to assist SMEs in obtaining and utilizing product data without excessive manual engineering efforts [1, 3]. This work focuses on working towards solving the issue of the manual high effort of finding the disassembly information within a given text and distilling the relevant aspects of a disassembly instruction such as needed tools, processes, positions, etc. into a structured depiction of different aspects to enable easy access for workers and inform automated disassembly processes with a structured, machine-readable format. The main contributions presented in this paper are: • A framework utilizing a hybrid approach of Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models for the extraction of textual information from manuals into a structured format, specifically for disassembly processes • A framework using solely the capabilities of Large Language Models to structure the textual information of disassembly processes into the same format as the hybrid approach. • An approach to structure disassembly information and an approach to evaluate the performance of extraction frameworks on this structure. • An experimental evaluation of the two presented frameworks on a newly created dataset of manuals and their disassembly instructions annotated with six categories of information elements. 2. State of the Art Disassembly sequence planning (DSP) is a critical operation in the closed-loop supply chain, as it determines the order of operations required to retrieve valuable components or materials from end-of-life (EOL) products. Effective DSP can significantly reduce the environmental footprint of manufacturing by facilitating the reuse of high-value parts. Historically, research in DSP has focused on several key modeling methodologies to represent the relationships between components and the constraints of physical disassembly. The literature identifies Graph-based, AND/OR Graph, Petri Net (PN) and Matrix-based modeling as primary modelling categories used in modern disassembly research [7]. While these modeling methods have matured, they often require a structured representation of the product's assembly as an input. In many real-world scenarios, especially for SMEs dealing with diverse EOL products, the only available information is the textual manual. This creates a critical research gap: how to bridge the divide between natural language disassembly instructions and the structured input required for DSP models. The rapid advancement of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) has presented a timely opportunity to address this gap. These technologies have become significantly more sophisticated in recent years, making them prime candidates for automating the extraction of technical knowledge. This paper introduces and evaluates a strategy to transform unstructured natural language from disassembly manuals into a curated, machine-readable format. Previous research in complex fields like construction and medicine has actively compared traditional rule-based parsers against statistical machine learning models. These studies highlight that neither method performs flawlessly in isolation, as they each struggle with different aspects of unstructured data. For instance, while rule-based systems offer high precision for specific entities, they often lack the broad flexibility of learning-based models. Ultimately, the literature suggests that a hybrid approach, combining the strict logic of rules with the adaptability of smart models, consistently yields the best results [8–10]. In accordance with these findings this paper attempts to uncover the implications of applying rule-based parsers and statistical machine learning models to text-like representations of disassembly information and subsequently accurately and consistently extract the instructions within. 3. Implementation To extract structured disassembly plans from unstructured manuals developed two extraction frameworks were developed, a rule-based NLP Parser and a GenAI extractor. The NLP Parser attempts to infer the correct labelling for each part of a disassembly instruction by utilizing a set of linguistic rules and analysis of the sentence structure. The GenAI extractor is given a system prompt which describes the process of determining the contents of each disassembly instruction. Fig. 1. Pipeline for extracting Disassembly instructions 3.1. Database The disassembly information can possess many forms such as a variety of video-, picture-, or text-data formats. Since this work focuses exclusively on text-data, the input for the two frameworks is constrained to text formats. The file formats to convey these texts are various. This paper focuses on only one, however files from any filetype that can have text extracted from it, can be utilized with this implementation and simply must replace the conversion into text with its own. A common format to convey text, particularly for manuals and Tim Schnieders et. al./ Procedia CIRP 00 (2026) 000–000 3 handling instructions for products, is the PDF format. Therefore, this data format lends itself to a comparison of instruction extraction techniques. 3.2. Output format The output format shall be structured, have easily identifiable categories and be able to be read into machines without any further language processing to facilitate an access point from which to go either towards full automation or a standardized instruction structure for humans. To address these needs the output has been defined as a table of regularly occurring elements of a disassembly instruction. These categories, called instruction categories in this research, include: • Action: The action being taken, expressed as a verb lemma optionally combined with a particle or directional adverb. (e.g. remove, unscrew, disconnect, snap off etc.) • Object: The component or part that the action is performed on. (e.g. screws, bolts, cover, panel, bearing etc.) • Tool: The tool or instrument used to perform the action, if specified. (e.g. Phillips screwdriver, flat-head screwdriver, T-27 Torx wrench, hammer, brass drift punch etc.) • Count: The quantity of objects involved, if explicitly stated. (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, two, three, four etc.) • Condition: A temporal, conditional, or simultaneous clause that constrains when or how the action is performed. (e.g. "after the system has completely shut down", "while pushing clip to the right", "once the spring pack is approximately halfway out" etc.) • Position: The spatial relationship describing where the action takes place or where the object is located/moved from. (e.g. "from bin body", "on the display head", "in lower right corner", "into a soft-jaw vise" etc.) The categories were determined by analyzing current research into disassembly planning methods, resulting in the categories Action; Object; Tool and Position. Reading through the available dataset revealed that these texts commonly contain other information that can potentially inform the disassembly process and help robotic or manual disassembly in defining the task, specifically Count and Condition. 3.3. Pre-Processing The input data consists of unstructured disassembly manuals, containing elements like diagrams, tables, instructions and safety warnings. The goal for this work is to compare the NLP Parser and the GenAI Extractor specifically on text data. Thus, preprocessing of the available manuals is necessary. First the data was transformed from PDF format into structured Markdown content using the Docling python library [11]. Second, the text was filtered for disassembly information from the Markdown using Gemini 2.5 Flash. This ensures that both approaches have a data input of plain text that is filtered to exclude other information, less relevant to disassembly planning, such as explanations of Legal Disclaimers, Product features, Cleaning and Maintenance as well as Warranty information. 3.4. Extraction The rule-based NLP Parser was developed using the spaCy library, which provides part-of-speech tags, lemmas, and dependency parse trees for each sentence [12]. This information is used to fill in the instruction category. To that end, syntactic patterns were defined to extract information when grammatical rules are met. It achieves extraction by analyzing the sentence in two passes. In the first pass, the patterns "use  to " are detected and the tool for later attachment is stored. In the second pass, all verbs whose dependency role within the spacy library are either ROOT, conj, xcomp, advcl, or ccomp are analyzed. For each verb, signaling a separate action, the categories contents are extracted in the following ways: • Action: the verb lemma, extended with any verbal particle (e.g. "pull out") or directional adverb (e.g. "turn clockwise"). • Object: built from spaCy's noun chunks. During training, one recurring issue was the ambiguity of the word "and". Splitting sentences on "and" sometimes correctly separated two instructions, but in other cases incorrectly split objects that belong together. This issue was solved by avoiding splitting by solely detecting "and", and instead use spaCy's dependency parse to detect joined objects (e.g., "plug and packing") via the .conjuncts function, expanding them into separate instructions, sharing the same action. • Tool: either found in first pass, otherwise from prepositional children such as "using", "with", "via", or "by" while skipping "followed by" which does not describe a tool. • Count: identified by the numeric modifier in the object's subtree. • Condition: extracted using a regex for temporal markers (e.g., "after", "before", "once"), with a fallback to dependencies that searches for prep labels. • Position: selected from prepositional phrases attached to the object or verb. Prepositions that indicate tools or ownership (e.g. "of", "with", "by", "using") are excluded from position candidates. The GenAI Extractor was developed based on an API that accesses Gemini 2.5 Flash. This model was chosen as an accessible API and promising results in preliminary test. The GenAI Extractor is separate from pre-processing and utilizes a different prompt for extracting instruction categories. We also provided examples to support Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning [13, 14]. The CoT workflow includes the role assignment, "You are an AI assistant acting as technical advisor for disassembly manuals", as well as Step-by-step task instructions in the form of a numbered list telling the model how to think through the document: 4 Tim Schnieders et. al./ Procedia CIRP 00 (2026) 000–000 • Carefully read through the markdown text of the manual. • Identify and extract all disassembly steps, ignoring safety warnings, legal texts. • Look for numbered lists and tables containing steps. • Ensure that each disassembly step is unique; do not include duplicates. • Always give the whole sentence for each step. • Only include disassembly steps, not reassembly or assembly. • Disassembly steps may include non-disassembly information that might look like assembly instructions but are still considered disassembly. The CoT also includes explicit rules for irregularities such as double-count prevention, typo fixing, pronoun resolution, and tool hallucination prevention as well as category definitions with constraints on what each category means and what to include or exclude. Few-shot demonstrations were added to the prompt showing two standard examples and four edge cases showing input and expected output for the model. The specific implementation is publicized under the name “Neuro-symbolic-extraction-framework” and can be found under the GitHub-link https://t.co/F0XM2ykbuV. 4. Evaluation To evaluate both frameworks, a custom evaluator was created that compares extraction outputs against a manually annotated target set. The work included for a human to manually annotate 741 instructions across 22 real-world disassembly manuals as ground truth. For each instruction, the six extraction categories were annotated: Action, Object, Count, Tool, Condition, and Position. The annotation treats each action as a separate instruction. This pertains specifically to occurrences of one sentence combining multiple instructions and for combined actions that apply the action to two different objects. Since the two frameworks do not necessarily produce the same number of instructions as the ground truth, rudimentary index-based comparison is not possible. A Best-Match alignment, which is a greedy many-to-one matching where every prediction is matched to the target with the highest Jaccard similarity, was utilized. Multiple predictions may map to the same target [15]. This allows for extra instructions describing the disassembly steps in more detail instead of penalizing them as spurious, as shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 2. Greedy many-to-one matching To establish a coherent terminology human annotated results for the instructions are defined as targets with a subscript i for the index of each match found in the greedy many-to-one matching, and j for the index of the instruction category, ti, j. The predictions of the models are annotated with the same subscript, pi, j. Both these variables can consist of a set of multiple tokens. For each matched pair, the six categories are compared individually. If both the predicted and target values are identical, the category scores 1.0. If one is empty and the other is not, the category scores 0.0. For partial matches, we award the category scores between 0.0 and 1.0 via Jaccard similarity, on token overlap, as shown in equation 1. Additionally, the per- category Jaccard similarity average across all matched rows is reported. These include precision P (equation 2), recall R (equation 3), F1 score (equation 4) and exact match EM (equation 5) [16]. The experiments in this paper are carried out under the Windows 11 64-Bit operating system, the CPU is an 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-11800H, 2.30 GHz, with 15,7 GB usable RAM. The program is executed in Visual Studio Code on Python 3.14.3. 5. Results The frameworks were evaluated on a corpus of real-world disassembly manuals comprising 741 manually annotated instructions. The manuals cover a range of products including consumer electronics (monitors, chargers), industrial machinery (wheelset bearings, differential assemblies), and household appliances. The results were reported using the Best-Match alignment, including coverage and per- category Jaccard similarity, as described in the evaluation section. FAKE NEWS ALERT 🚨

Claim (Adil Raja)@soldierspeaks
According to an unverified intelligence claim, Field Marshal Asim Munir shared sensitive Chinese technological information with the United States, angering Beijing and risking Pakistan’s most important strategic partnership.

What the evidence actually shows

The claim originates solely from Adil Raja’s own “sources.” He himself labels it an unverified intelligence claim.

As recently as 2 November 2026, Field Marshal Asim Munir met Chinese CPC Minister Liu Haixing at GHQ Rawalpindi. Both sides publicly reaffirmed the “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership” and discussed strengthening cooperation. Official ISPR and Chinese readouts contain no hint of anger over any technology transfer.

Pakistan-China defence and economic ties remain deep and active (CPEC 2.0, ongoing military cooperation, high-level exchanges). Routine Chinese concerns over the security of their personnel on CPEC projects are longstanding and unrelated to any alleged tech-sharing with Washington.

Adil Raja (former major, now UK-based) has a consistent pattern of sensational, source-based claims against the military leadership that are rarely, if ever, substantiated. Pakistan has designated him under anti-terrorism laws for anti-state propaganda.

Pakistan is balancing improved US ties (Trump’s public praise for Munir) with its traditional China relationship. No credible evidence exists of any betrayal of Chinese technology.

This is classic narrative-building dressed up as breaking intelligence. No proof has been offered because none exists in the public domain.

text:
Distrust between Iran and the US has deep historical roots, shaped by the 1953 coup d’état, the revolution and the hostage crisis. The US withdrawal from the JCPoA and subsequent attacks on Iran during negotiations have deepened that distrust to the point where, even if Tehran and Washington hypothetically began a love story, the rest of the world would struggle to trust the relationship.

Remaining constantly cautious and on alert serves neither the economic interests of regional actors nor those of the wider world. The unpredictable order Washington has helped create in the Middle East and beyond means that any assessment of economic prospects must account for the risk of renewed military tensions and war. That uncertainty discourages long-term investment.

One possible way forward for Tehran might be to establish economic ties with the US: not necessarily on a vast scale, but sufficient to give American businesses a meaningful stake inside Iran. Their presence could serve two purposes: 
First, it could signal to investors elsewhere that doing business with Iran is viable, provided sanctions relief is clear and credible, and help ease fears of punishment. 
Second, it could act as a barometer of military risk and a potential restraint on escalation: Washington might be more reluctant to attack while American citizens, businesses and investments were present in Iran.

Many Iranian hardliners might reject such an arrangement outright. Yet it could offer a measure of military and economic security, creating the stability needed for a new order to take shape. When confronting a wolf, sometimes the safer position may be close enough to make it harder for the animal to bite.

Such ties could also serve a longstanding US objective regarding Iran: reducing threats to the US and its allies. The relationship would create mutual interests in restraint, giving both Tehran and Washington more to lose from renewed confrontation.

🎯 MYANMAR COURTS WASHINGTON WITH RARE EARTH OFFER AS SUPPLY CHAIN RIVALRY DEEPENS

📍 NAYPYIDAW, MYANMAR

🟨 OUR ASSESSMENT: Chinese dominance in rare earths has always depended on more than domestic mines. It rests on control of processing, logistics and years of relationships across neighboring resource regions, including Myanmar. That makes Myanmar's appeal to Washington harder than a simple investment decision.

Any American effort to secure alternative supply chains would run into the reality that the most valuable deposits sit inside an active conflict zone where political authority is fragmented. Capital can enter quickly; stable control over extraction and transport cannot. The result is that supply chain diversification becomes a geopolitical problem before it becomes a mining project.

Even if new US investments materialize, breaking China's position would require processing capacity, transport networks and long-term security arrangements that take years to build. The immediate consequence may be more competition for influence in Myanmar's border regions rather than a rapid shift in global rare earth flows.

Iran has urged the United States to meet its conditions—including a two-day proposal and seven core demands—to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei, are pressing Washington to act on Tehran's conditions, which involve ending the war on all fronts and lifting the U.S. blockade.

Iran has offered to reopen the critical Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. lifts its blockade and the conflict officially concludes

“The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iran’s IRNA news agency.

“The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy, and address Iran’s demands and conditions — which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table.”

Tehran has proposed reopening Hormuz, which it has blockaded since the start of the war, within two days in return for Washington meeting a raft of conditions.

These include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Reacting, US president Trump, whose Republican party last week lost midterm elections in part due to the war, said on Monday that there was “positive momentum” toward ending the conflict after meeting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House.

In a post on social media, Trump reiterated that the US was “locked and loaded” but said further strikes were “quite unlikely” given that key US allies in the Gulf “would prefer the status quo.”

“We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected,” Trump said.

text:
Democratic approach to relations with China that should be adopted after the Midterm elections of 2026:

 China Jake Werner and Sandy Shan -The relationship between the world’s two most powerful countries will shape the global order for the next century. Over the last decade, as the leaders of the United States and China increasingly fixated on the threat posed by the other, they lost sight of that. Rather than asking how they could reshape the world system to safely accommodate both great powers, each sought to manipulate the system to gain a competitive advantage. In so doing, they began to transform the global order toward cutthroat geopolitical conflict. A zero-sum US–China relationship would undermine the possibility of progressive reform in both countries and beyond, sidelining hopes for economic equality, cultural inclusion, substantive democracy, and environmental sustainability.  At the same time, our current crisis offers a precious opportunity for deep structural changes that could stabilize US–China relations on the shared foundation of a more egalitarian global society. The task is fraught. Tensions with China have reshaped the US foreign policy consensus and reoriented a range of government institutions around a tendentious portrayal of Chinese success as incompatible with US values and interests. Antagonistic policies, legislation, and rhetoric proliferated while the shared interests that could connect the two countries were dismissed. These aggressive measures failed and China is now stronger, less dependent on the United States, and more aggrieved. US–China conflict arises not just from elite insecurity and great power nationalism, but also from the growth of zero-sum dynamics within the global system. Since the collapse of market-led globalization following 2008, slow growth and cost-of-living challenges have afflicted all countries because of the extreme levels of inequality that are common across them. Economic stagnation encourages us-or-them thinking, between countries as well as within them. Vilification is particularly tempting when it comes to the Chinese government, which is much more repressive today than a decade ago and which stands opposed to progressive values across a whole range of issues. It is worth asking whether a cooperation-minded government in the United States would even have a partner in Beijing. The chaos of President Donald Trump’s second term provides part of the answer. By destabilizing what was beginning to look like a permanent regime of great power conflict, Trump is scrambling the politics around US–China confrontation and battering the very institutions and alliances that the first Trump and Joe Biden administrations sought to organize against China. That has created space for a progressive alternative on China policy. As long as the United States and China avoid war during Trump’s term, China will continue to have a powerful interest in a stable geopolitical landscape, a prosperous and open global economy, and multilateral cooperation to address transnational dangers like climate change and pandemic disease.
 Some of China’s behavior undermines these aims, but much of its foreign policy supports such an order. One core goal of a constructive US–China relationship is to give Beijing a stake in responding to US pressure—something a combative relationship actively discourages. Contrary to conventional wisdom in Washington, China has a demonstrated lack of interest in playing the role of global hegemon.4 It has not  engaged in foreign military interventions since 1979. It has declined the many opportunities presented by US misadventures in the Middle East and Latin America to assert a military presence. It has not attempted to fill the leadership vacuum left by Washington in recent years. Its military spending has been at or below 2 percent of GDP for some three decades. That has sustained a major buildup in forces because of rapid economic growth, but China’s military concerns are overwhelmingly focused on its claim to Taiwan and, secondarily, efforts to influence nearby seas, rather than on projecting power far afield. Beijing’s limited ambition leaves open the possibility of US–China concord yet also means Washington will need to take the initiative in framing a global agenda. Everything turns on the US orientation in the period following Trump. Will a new US administration seek to split the world into two warring camps? Or will it throw its efforts into building a multipolar world in which interests are aligned through  positive-sum multilateral reform? Framing a new strategy The next administration can set the tone on day one by signaling a clear rejection of geopolitical bloc formation. The disintegration of world order since 2008 has left all countries facing crises of domestic political legitimacy and the breakdown of previously stable forms of economic growth. This common predicament has led all of them—very much including the United States and China—to act in counterproductive ways. Rather than looking for scapegoats and assigning blame, the key is to recognize that all are suffering from this crisis, and none can emerge from it except through an inclusive process of global reform. At the same time, the next administration must condemn counterproductive responses to the crisis and repudiate zero-sum behavior. This includes the pursuit of spheres of influence, the weaponization of economic relations to coerce other countries, nativist violence at home, nationalist belligerence abroad, manipulation of multilateral institutions for power politics, and an abdication of responsibility to act on the climate crisis. While China is guilty of all these practices, so is the United States. Effectively calling China to account will require the United States to get its own house in order. More than condemnation, however, the emphasis should be on positive opportunities to chart a path out of the chaos: reform to the systems of global growth and authority so that prosperity is no longer a zero-sum game. Framing the US–China relationship within a wider context of multilateral reform is necessary to break the US foreign policy establishment’s habit of viewing global issues as proxy battles in US–China conflict and to convince Beijing that the United States does not view Chinese success as a threat. Immediate actions Before the project of global reform can gain momentum, bilateral flashpoints will have to be addressed. China needs to be confident that its interests will be secure in the global order the United States seeks, and US leaders need to make some immediate progress on core interests like peace in the Western Pacific, ending the cycle of retaliatory economic attacks, and ensuring that Chinese economic growth does not undermine prosperity in the United States. The next administration should immediately prepare for a presidential- level meeting with China’s leader and begin the process of rebuilding the multilevel US–China economic and security diplomacy that was destroyed under Trump I and only halfheartedly revived under President Biden. The following key issues should be on the agenda: Clear support for the One China Policy, while opposing any unilateral alteration of the status quo across the Strait and accepting any resolution of the Taiwan question that is achieved peacefully. Serious Chinese aggression would be a cataclysm for the people of Taiwan and would disastrously destabilize regional politics and the global economy, sinking the possibility of progressive global reform. US measures to deter Chinese adventurism should therefore continue but must be balanced by stronger and more sincere efforts to reassure China that the United States is not pursuing permanent separation or exploiting Taiwan as a strategic asset. Such moves should be coordinated with US allies Japan and South Korea, both of which have legitimate concerns about Chinese belligerence but have also at times played on US hostility toward China to keep the United States engaged in the region. Going forward, the new administration should insist on a more restrained Chinese posture around Taiwan. While Beijing will not formally renounce the use of force on what it considers a core matter of national sovereignty, the United States can make clear that ratcheting down tension on its side will only proceed in tandem with reciprocal moves from China. Set a course to ending economic warfare against China. The first Trump administration very nearly destroyed China’s most successful multinational company, Huawei, and Biden systematized efforts to stifle China’s technological advance through extraterritorial export controls, ever-expanding blacklists of Chinese firms, and strong-arming allies to join the blockades. Attempts are also underway to force third countries to exclude Chinese trade and investment. These efforts not only failed on their own terms, but they also inspired China to build up its own regime of extraterritorial economic coercion. As the second Trump administration has reluctantly come to understand, the United States and China now stand in an economic balance of terror. A new administration should lay out an economic “arms control” agenda to limit weaponized interdependence, with the aim of moving toward abolition of these dangerous economic weapons. The process can start with bilateral US–China negotiations, since these two have taken the weaponization process furthest, but agreement on new rules should eventually connect with the broader multilateral reform negotiations discussed below.  Normalize the presence of China in the US economy. The China panic in Washington has led to widespread prohibitions on Chinese investment in the United States. That risks significant damage to the US economy because Chinese businesses are increasingly sophisticated in technology, design, and industrial organization. If US companies are indefinitely cut off from contact with Chinese producers and shielded from their competitive pressure, they will increasingly cede global markets to Chinese firms as well as the European and Asian competitors that have not severed the connection to China. This self-harm is particularly threatening to the US climate transition because Chinese companies are at the cutting edge of electric vehicles, batteries, and clean energy. A joint venture framework welcoming Chinese investment in the United States offers a solution. Chinese industrial producers would gain market access to the United States in exchange for accepting conditions on their investment, including taking a joint venture partner, transferring technology and know-how to their partners, a union neutrality agreement opening the way to organizing workers, and supply chain localization. Foreground the problem of Chinese overcapacity but reframe it as a global economic problem that requires coordinated changes in policy. The Biden and second Trump administrations criticized Chinese overproduction arising from nonmarket economic practices, which they say distorts the global economy and threatens industry in the United States and elsewhere. The indictment has substantial merit, but because its aim is to discredit China rather than resolve the global economic dysfunctions that produce Chinese behavior, it ends up spurring a defensive reaction on China’s part and poisoning diplomacy. The next administration should reframe the problem. Rather than arguing that the world has too much wealth, it should recognize that the world has too much privation. Where “overproduction” insists on diminishing one party or another, “underconsumption” motivates a search for ways to expand purchasing power, potentially extending the benefits worldwide. Once again, bilateral problems in the US–China relationship only become tractable when placed in the proper context of a broken global system. China has much to contribute to fixing that system. The “nonmarket” policies it pioneered—shaping markets to serve goals beyond profit— are crucial to overcoming the stark limitations on development imposed by market dogma. Far too few countries enjoy the capacity, resources, and impunity from “free trade” rules to pursue the kind of industrial policy that China used to achieve a developmental breakthrough. China could help rectify this injustice. Yet its leaders, feeling besieged by criticism from the West, have missed this opportunity and instead insist that domestic overcapacity poses no danger to other countries and that its own policies are purely market oriented. Facing fierce competition and geopolitical tensions, they have also resisted steps to raise wages faster or increase spending on collective goods. Without steps to significantly increase the labor share of output, wider adoption of industrial policy would only exacerbate global economic dysfunction. The solution is laid out below. A four-year agenda of global reform These initial measures would not resolve all major points of friction overnight, but they would mark a clear departure from the antagonism of recent years and begin reestablishing the trust required for deeper bilateral cooperation. The worldwide breakdown of multilateralism during Trump’s second term has revealed the fragility of today’s global architecture. The next administration has a rare opportunity not merely to mend these institutions but to rebuild the global system on firmer, fairer foundations, and to engage China as a central partner in constructing that new order. The following actions would not only begin to repair the wreckage coming out of Trump II but also establish a new structure of egalitarian global growth and integration needed to overcome the crises of the post-2008 period: Work with China to reform global economic governance. A progressive US strategy must reorient its approach by abandoning efforts to weaponize the Bretton Woods institutions (BWIs)—the core multilateral financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank— against China and instead working with Beijing to reform them. Beijing has increased its own capital contributions while joining many Global South countries in demanding greater voice, more equitable representation, and a stronger project emphasis on sustainable infrastructure and industrial upgrading.
 These priorities align closely with the broader project of building a more balanced and inclusive global economy. Two immediate priorities stand out. First, the United States should reject the narrative that China is chiefly responsible for the debilitating debt burden in much of the Global South and instead work with Beijing through the Group of 20 process to build a fairer architecture for debt relief. Well-founded concerns about transparency and coordination among diverse creditors can only be addressed by good-faith engagement.8 Second, reviving the legitimacy of the BWIs depends on long-delayed governance reforms that expand representation for Global South countries, but developed countries have used China as an excuse to block progress. Breaking this gridlock is essential if BWIs are to function as credible institutions in a multipolar world. Finally, the United States should support deeper cooperation between the BWIs and China-backed institutions, publicly affirming China’s development efforts as a contribution toward a more multipolar order with wider legitimacy. By remaining outside major China-backed initiatives, Washington only diminishes its own influence. Restore US climate leadership by acknowledging our historical responsibilities, embracing more ambitious goals, and forging a genuine partnership with China to advance global climate action. As the United States reenters the Paris Agreement on climate, it must revive the cooperative spirit between Washington and Beijing that made the original accord possible. A central step is ending the practice of using China as a convenient foil to deflect from the United States’s historical responsibility for carbon emissions. The rest of the world is not deceived, and that approach only pushes China into a defensive posture focused on achieving recognition of its contributions rather than on advancing more ambitious and proactive measures. A renewed approach to US climate leadership must instead focus on unlocking the full potential of joint climate action between the United States and China. That begins with pursuing opportunities for joint US–China climate finance for the Global South, where the success of the global energy transition will ultimately be decided. Coordinated financing for renewable infrastructure, grid modernization, and industrial upgrading would deliver far greater impact than parallel or competing initiatives. Revolutionize global development and pull China into the project. Momentum on the BWIs and climate action should build toward deeper change. Three core reforms are needed: strong global labor standards, a worldwide system for the provision of public goods, and large-scale development finance.
 The first and second would bolster the security and bargaining power of working people, forcing capital away from speculation and the race to the bottom and into high-standards productive investment. The second and third would ensure that higher standards do not exclude developing countries from global growth. Together, these three structural reforms could drive a productivity breakthrough that could underwrite long-term egalitarian growth. These aims are compatible with China’s domestic reform agenda and its goal of cultivating support in the Global South, but China will not seek a system with the necessary scope and ambition on its own. Should China prove a reluctant partner, the United States would take the credit alone for proposing reforms that finally meet the expectations of the Global South. If China joined in, global development would gain considerable impetus. US and Chinese development models are distinct but complementary, each meeting needs the other leaves unmet. To fully realize the potential, the United States should engage host countries and other stakeholders from the outset and include China in these consultations to improve coordination and align development finance with host countries’ priorities. A new approach to human rights, democracy, and pluralism The worldwide growth of openly authoritarian, racist, nativist, and misogynistic political currents has eroded the classical liberal concept of human rights that dominated the market-led globalization era. In that period, democracy and multiculturalism were embraced in ideology but not in substance, while oligarchic inequality not only betrayed the promise of the creed but cultivated popular cynicism about its very plausibility.

 Establishing the egalitarian global system described above would provide the basis for a new era of human rights victories in the United States, China, and around the world. But in this process, human rights diplomacy will need to change. The US approach should not hinge on isolating and punishing China. The United States should make clear that, although it stands proudly behind a vision of deep political and economic democracy as the best system for all people, it also believes that such a system can never be imposed on other societies and that each country will chart its own path. The United States should foreswear the tutelary role it assumed in the “end of history” era as well as the “authoritarianism versus democracy” framework that Biden deployed against China.15 As we now know all too well, reactionary political currents are present in every country regardless of its political regime, and pretending  otherwise only makes them stronger. Geopolitical rivalry inevitably breeds authoritarian reflexes, heightens repression of domestic dissent, and narrows the political space for civil society on all sides. These effects have been visible in both the United States and China over the last decade. Instead of using human rights as a cudgel against adversaries, the United States should hold itself to the same standards it demands of China. Doing so reframes democracy as a shared global struggle rather than a “Western value” wielded for strategic advantage. This would undermine Beijing’s claim that democracy and human rights are simply a tool of US domination. At the same time, the United States should further strengthen pathways and protections for individuals fleeing persecution by the Chinese government. Meaningful engagement with Chinese diaspora communities and other grassroots US organizations, instead of symbolic gestures, anchors policy in solidarity rather than suspicion. Broadening participation in foreign policymaking is thus not only consistent with democratic practice, but also essential to ensuring that solutions to geopolitical conflict do not amplify xenophobia or erode civil liberties. The United States was never capable of bestowing genuine democracy on China and certainly cannot do so now that we are fighting for the survival of our own. But a humbler United States, with a clearer understanding that our similarities with China are stronger than our differences, could motivate a far more transformative agenda than we ever saw in the age of unipolar hubris.

text:
Lake Bachar: Pirates A-to-Z

I have a real soft spot for the game’s weirdos. Lake Bachar is one of those guys. Beyond his unique appearance lies an equally unique backstory befitting a dude who would look at home at a GWAR concert or Cryptid Con.

But make no mistake -- when your starter is out of the game in the 4th inning and your offense has somehow still kept you in the game, Bachar is the guy you want to see making the walk from the bullpen to give you a fighting chance. And how he got here is a pretty interesting tale. 

Revisiting The Origin Story

Relievers often have a circuitous journeys to the major leagues. But even by that measure, Bachar’s road to Pittsburgh was pretty unlikely. 

Continuing the football theme started with yesterday’s profile on Braxton Ashcraft, who was an incredible wide receiver in high school, Lake Bachar was originally a kicker. A graduate of Wheaton North High School in Illinois, he attended the famous University of Wisconsin-Whitewater, where he was an all-conference punter for the Division III football team.

I say famous because the UW–Whitewater Warhawks made history as the first school in NCAA history (in any division) to win a three-sport national sweep in a single academic year, claiming national titles in football, basketball, and baseball in 2013–14.

In fact, Bachar kicked 3 FGs in the 2014 Stagg Bowl to help the Warhawks win that national championship as a sophomore. There’s absolutely another version of his story where he ends up a kicker in the NFL. But then, his flowing long hair would spend most Sundays under a helmet. And that would be a damn shame.

Instead, the two-sport star in high school found that the extra muscle he’d added for football helped his fastball inch up past 90 mph. He walked on to his college baseball team and ended up dominating in a second sport, getting drafted by the Padres in the 5th round of the 2016 draft.

You read that right. Bachar was drafted way back in 2016 as a 21-year old and spent 8 years bouncing around the minor leagues before debuting as a reliever for the Marlins at age 29 in 2024. Yo-yoing as a starter and reliever, his slider and curveball were standout pitches that kept him getting opportunities.

He was the #29/30 ranked prospect for the Padres when he underwent a Tommy John surgery in 2021 and was later released as a minor league free agent in 2023. Re-signed with the Padres, he was later selected off waivers by Miami where he appeared in 10 games for the Marlins in 2024. 

He returned to their bullpen in 2025 and went 8-2 with a 3.95 ERA -- numbers he’d repeat in 2026 before being traded to the Pirates at the deadline this past August.

Looking Back at 2026

Of course, as we all know, the signature challenge for the 2026 Pirates was a miserable bullpen for two solid months way too early in the season to do much about it. When your entire bullpen falls apart in early May, with 10 blown saves for losses over a two month period, there isn’t much recourse.

By the time Bachar was being traded to the Pirates on August 3 in exchange for Brandan Bidois, Hyun Seung Lee and Brian Sanchez, the team was already basically out of it. The remainder of that month would hammer that nail deeper, but it was already there that final day of the trade deadline.

Still, it was refreshing to suddenly have a sparkly new bullpen. Bachar was not supposed to be the highlight of the four that came in, but he absolutely was. His 2.57 ERA across 15 appearances, including eight as opener, was pretty strong. He achieved a 0.9 WAR for the Pirates in just 28.0 IP with 32 K and an impressive ability to limit contact.

He took over for Carmen Mlodzinski as the team’s opener during the nearly two-month period of covering for Mitch Keller’s spot in the rotation after he went down with his injury in early August. 

Across both teams in 2026, he had a 78th percentile xERA of 3.39 and a 90th percentile xBA of .199. With fairly pedestrian velocity and offspeed stuff, his breaking offerings are legit elite and led to an outstanding whiff rate, K rate and hard-hit rate.

He was a welcomed addition to the bullpen, for sure.

On the Horizon -- 2027 & Beyond

Suffice it to say, Bachar’s unlikely journey to the major leagues finds him as a 31-year old reliever for the Pirates who won’t be arbitration eligible until 2028 in his age 33 season. Sometimes the sport is funny that way.

Relievers are traditionally failed starters who may look a little funny on paper. Bachar’s utilitarian history prepares him well as a bulk reliever who may eventually settle in as a RH middle reliever for the Pirates. So long as he continues placing his curveball and slider, there’s no reason to think he can’t be a bedrock of the bullpen.

But relievers without strong fastballs have a way of hitting lulls. Just look to Dennis Santana last year as a cautionary tale -- another scrap heap bullpen guy who excelled until he suddenly didn’t. I’m not wishing that juju on anyone, but we have to be realistic and clear-eyed about these late bloomers.

I am mostly hopeful Bachar can repeat his 2026 success, with a 3.25-3.50 ERA and a lot of multi-inning relief appearances where he continues limiting hard contact. There will always be a role for a guy like that.

A Final Word

All signs are pointing to a much better bullpen for the Pirates in 2027, and Bachar appears to be one of the guys who will be penciled in as a component piece. 

I can’t help but see him as the sort of player the deal being offered by the owners to the MLBPA is meant to serve. Bachar won’t be a free agent until 2031 following his age 36 season. When you think about who would benefit most from an increased minimum salary and a shortened runway to free agency, it’s a guy like Bachar.

For now, he’s exactly the archetype a small market team like the Pirates covet -- a seasoned specialist who is inexpensive and dependable. 

Oh, and the hair. This column is only scratching the surface as Bachar is a pretty intriguing dude. He’s into the paranormal and ghost hunting. He calls his hairstyle “the lettuce.” There’s a lot here.

We’ll unpack these mysteries in a future installment, no doubt.

text:
A ₹85,000 wearable that sits on the temple, not the wrist, and aims to track blood flow to the brain.

Temple, the health-tech venture of Zomato co-founder Deepinder Goyal, opened pre-orders on 1 November. It's one of the most talked-about health gadgets in India this year, and one of the most debated.

Here's what it is, what the evidence shows so far, and what it doesn't.

🧠 What Temple is

A small, pebble-shaped device worn on the side of the head, between the eye and the ear. No screen, no strap. It sticks on with adhesive patches called Grips and talks to a phone app.

It uses optical sensors (PPG), the same basic light-based technique smartwatches use for heart rate. The difference is where it sits.

It reports two headline metrics:

BrainFlow: a signal intended to track relative changes in blood circulation to the brain.

Entropy: a proprietary score from 1 to 250, updated every second, meant to reflect how hard the body is working. Goyal describes it as "the price the body pays to survive at a given moment".

🔍 The question it's trying to answer

Smartwatches and rings track heart rate, sleep, HRV, steps and stress estimates. None of them directly track circulation in the head.

Temple asks a different question: how does blood supply to the brain change when we exercise, sleep, sit for hours, get stressed or change posture?

The brain is one of the body's most energy-hungry organs, and it depends on a constant supply of oxygen and glucose through the blood. So it's a genuinely interesting thing to want to measure.

⚠️ The core scientific challenge

The temple sits over the superficial temporal artery. That's a branch of the external carotid, which mainly supplies the scalp and face.

The brain itself is fed mainly by the internal carotid and vertebral arteries, sitting under skin, bone and fluid.

So a sensor on the skin there has to separate scalp blood from brain blood. That's the heart of the debate.

There's another wrinkle. The brain has a built-in system called cerebral autoregulation, which keeps its blood flow fairly steady across everyday changes in posture and blood pressure. So the signals Temple is chasing are subtle.

📊 What the company's own studies show

BrainFlow vs time-domain NIRS: TD-NIRS times how long light takes to travel through tissue, which lets researchers separate deeper brain signals from shallower scalp ones.

In a study guided by Boston University's Prof. David Boas, with 44 healthy young men and 60 sessions, BrainFlow correlated with brain blood volume at r = 0.84 to 0.91 across posture challenges. In head-down tilt, the correlation was 0.91 with the brain and 0.49 with the scalp.

BrainFlow vs transcranial Doppler: in 23 healthy adults, a within-person correlation of about 0.8 with blood-flow velocity in a major brain artery, during cycling and posture changes.

Heart rate: in a treadmill study of 43 healthy adults aged 20 to 35, against a Polar H10 chest strap, Temple reported an average error of 1.18 bpm. Apple Watch Series 12 came in at 1.94, WHOOP MG 3.14, Garmin Forerunner 970 3.18 and Oura Ring 5 at 5.21.

The important caveat: Temple funded, ran and analysed these studies. The brain studies are preprints, not yet peer reviewed. The heart-rate test covered treadmill running only, not cycling, strength training or outdoor runs. And a correlation in a lab is not the same as accuracy in daily life.

🗣️ The debate

Several doctors have questioned whether a skin sensor at the temple can measure brain blood flow at all, rather than circulation in the scalp and face.

Critics have also challenged the "Entropy" name, since entropy has specific meanings in physics and biology, and Goyal's earlier "Gravity Ageing Hypothesis", which links gravity, brain blood flow and ageing.

Goyal's response: Temple is "strictly a fitness + AI device", makes no medical claims, and isn't meant to diagnose or prevent disease. He has offered devices to independent researchers, said the company will fund replication, and urged sceptical buyers to wait for that independent validation.

He also advised people to get the basics right first, sleep, diet, strength training, sprinting and daily walking, before spending on advanced trackers. Good advice, whoever it comes from.

🧩 How it compares

Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, Garmin and WHOOP are mature, wrist-based trackers for heart rate, sleep, activity and recovery.

Head-worn devices aren't new either. The Muse headband measures electrical brain activity (EEG). Kernel Flow is a research headset built on time-domain NIRS.

Temple's bet is a small, continuously worn consumer device focused on circulation-related signals. Something different rather than something more, and potentially a complement to existing wearables, not a replacement.

💰 Price and ownership

₹85,000, including the device, a charging pod, a lifetime supply of Grips and lifetime app access with no subscription. Batch 01 is handmade to order, with delivery expected around three months after ordering. Goyal has said he expects India to be a small share of global sales.

Temple has offered a 14-day return policy in India, and Goyal has said that may change.

❓ Questions worth asking before buying

Has BrainFlow been independently validated and peer reviewed?
Does it show relative changes or absolute blood flow?
How does it perform during real sport, not just a treadmill?
Does Entropy predict anything useful, or is it a new number to watch?
Can a doctor interpret the data?
What happens to that data, and who owns it?

🎓 The takeaway

Temple is asking a genuinely new question: can a consumer sensor track how everyday life affects the brain's blood supply?

The early, company-run evidence is interesting. But it isn't yet independent, peer-reviewed proof, and the device can't diagnose anything or show whether someone's brain circulation is healthy.

The next 12 to 24 months of independent testing will say far more than any launch post.

GRAB $GRAB — A $750M AI INFRASTRUCTURE COMMITMENT COULD CHANGE THE INVESTMENT STORY. BUT WILL IT CREATE SHAREHOLDER VALUE?
I've been reviewing Grab's latest SEC filing, and this is a significant development.
Grab, SoftBank and PETROS have signed joint development agreements to build AI infrastructure in Malaysia, with $1.85B in proposed initial seed capital and a long-term capacity ambition of at least 5 GW.
THE KEY NUMBERS
🔹 Combined Proposed Seed Capital: $1.85B
🔹 SoftBank: $1.0B
🔹 Grab: $750M
🔹 PETROS: $100M
🔹 Long-Term Capacity Target: 5 GW+
🔹 Grab Q3 Net Cash Liquidity: $5.0B
🔹 Grab Q3 Adjusted EBITDA: $237M (+73% YoY)
🔹 Grab TTM Adjusted FCF: $533M
WHAT'S CHANGING
Grab is potentially expanding beyond its established Southeast Asian mobility, delivery and financial-services ecosystem into capital-intensive AI infrastructure.
The opportunity is interesting. Malaysia offers a strategic location for regional AI capacity, while SoftBank brings experience and relationships across the technology investment ecosystem.
But the 5 GW target is a long-term ambition, not installed capacity.
The agreements include binding development and funding obligations, while final investment terms and project execution remain subject to further agreements and conditions.
THE INVESTMENT QUESTION
Grab's core business is improving. Revenue is growing, adjusted EBITDA is expanding and cash generation is strengthening.
That's encouraging.
But committing substantial capital to AI infrastructure introduces a different set of risks.
Power availability, construction timelines, customer commitments, financing costs and utilisation will determine whether these projects generate attractive returns.
I also want to understand how this investment affects Grab's existing capital allocation priorities, including share repurchases.
MY TAKE
I've followed Grab for some time, and I continue to see attractive long-term potential in its Southeast Asian platform.
This announcement could create another growth opportunity, but I'm not automatically treating it as bullish simply because AI infrastructure is involved.
The $750M commitment is substantial, and the economics need to justify the capital.
For me, the critical distinction is between announcing AI capacity and generating profitable returns from deployed infrastructure.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Can Grab and its partners secure the customers, power, financing and utilisation needed to turn this ambitious AI infrastructure plan into sustainable free cash flow and attractive returns on invested capital?

text:
A lamb with a gut full of worms will walk past the good grass to eat a bitter plant that kills them, and the only place it ever learned which plant was at its mother's side.

Researchers at Utah State University spent years watching this, because nobody believed it. They took lambs carrying a heavy load of stomach worms and offered them two feeds. Plain alfalfa, which a lamb loves. And alfalfa laced with tannins, the bitter, mouth-drying compound that makes stewed tea undrinkable and that happens to be hard on gut parasites. Healthy lambs barely touched the bitter one. Why would they.

The wormy lambs started eating it. Then preferring it. They ate more of the medicine the sicker they were, and their worm counts fell. Then the researchers dosed them with a proper wormer, the parasites went, and the lambs went straight back to the plain feed. They took the medicine while they were ill and stopped when they were cured, which is more than can be said for most of the people in a pharmacy queue.

The second part is the one that should keep a dietitian up at night. They put lambs on a heavy, bitter diet and offered them a compound that neutralises the bitterness. Lambs that fed alongside their mothers learned to take it. Lambs taken away from their mothers never touched it. Not once. The knowledge of what to eat when something is wrong was being handed down at the trough, ewe to lamb, by example, and a lamb without its mother simply never got the lesson.

Shepherds have known a version of this for as long as there have been shepherds. The sick ewe that goes off on her own to the hedge bottom and eats something she ignores the rest of the year. The flock that heads for the rough corner of the field in a wet spring. Nobody wrote it down because it was obvious.

In 1928 a doctor in Chicago let babies choose their own food from a tray, and the one with rickets drank cod liver oil until his bones healed and then stopped. It is the same experiment, with wool on.

Meanwhile the human version of the lamb is handed a plate diagram, a list of recommended portions and a leaflet on overriding cravings, and told the instinct is the thing that needs managing.

The lamb was never given a diagram.

It had its mother, a hedge, and enough sense to stop taking the tablets when it was better.

text:
Crypto Is Growing Up. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen Says Its Security Model Needs to Grow Up Too.

For years, cryptocurrency exchanges have operated as all-in-one platforms, allowing users to store assets, execute trades, and access financial products in one place. That convenience helped make crypto more accessible, but it also created a security model that is becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
In this episode of Drops, I sit down with @Bitget CEO, @GracyBitget, to discuss the security challenges facing crypto exchanges, the lessons from Bitget's recent $388 million breach, and why she believes separating custody from trading could represent an important step forward for the industry.

A $388 Million Wake-Up Call

On September 24, Bitget experienced a major security breach involving unauthorized transfers of approximately $388 million from its hot and warm wallets. The initial suspicious transfers began around 2:30 a.m. in Gracy’s time zone, followed by larger withdrawals shortly afterward. She happened to wake up before 4 a.m., checked her phone, and discovered what was unfolding.
Her immediate priorities were understanding the extent of the losses, identifying the vulnerability, and determining whether the threat had been contained. Within hours, she was addressing the community publicly, even as the investigation continued. The experience was emotionally demanding, and Gracy admits there were moments when her hands shook, despite her efforts to remain composed.

"I'm a human being. I'm not an AI," she said.

The breach originated through third-party vulnerabilities rather than compromised private keys, and Bitget's cold wallets remained secure. The company subsequently patched vulnerabilities, strengthened withdrawal procedures, and used its existing protection fund to cover the losses, leaving customer balances unaffected.
But beyond the immediate response, Gracy came away with a more fundamental realization: Improving security protocols alone would not solve the underlying problem.

Why the Traditional Exchange Model Is Reaching Its Limits

To understand Gracy's argument, it helps to understand how centralized cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Unlike conventional financial markets, where different institutions handle trading, custody, and clearing, crypto exchanges have often combined these functions. Gracy describes this structure as "one giant monster."

The advantage is a seamless experience where users can deposit funds, purchase assets, move between products, and execute trades, but the problem is that concentrating so many responsibilities within one organization also concentrates risk. As exchanges expand their offerings, they create more systems, dependencies, and potential vulnerabilities to protect from, while attackers only need to exploit one weakness to cause substantial damage.

Gracy argues that this creates an inherently uneven contest between security teams and hackers, especially as attacks become increasingly sophisticated. Her conclusion is that the industry needs to reconsider its architecture rather than simply keep adding protective measures to the same underlying model.

The Open Custody Network

Gracy's proposed solution is the Bitget Open Custody Network, which she summarizes in one sentence as "Assets in bank, trading on Bitget." Essentially, customers would no longer need to keep all their assets directly with the exchange to trade on its platform. Instead, custody would move to specialized providers, including established banks, digital banks, and dedicated cryptocurrency custody firms. Bitget would continue facilitating trading, while these separate institutions would be responsible for safeguarding customer assets.

However, separating custody from trading introduces its own considerations. Customers must understand the custodian's regulatory status, financial strength, security record, jurisdiction, and the time or cost involved in accessing funds. The model is intended to distribute responsibilities, thus reducing risk.

Security Comes With a Trade-Off

Crypto users have become accustomed to moving funds almost instantly, and introducing independent custodians could make certain processes slower or more complicated. This may be acceptable for institutional investors who often prioritize asset protection over convenience, but retail customers may see things differently.

Gracy acknowledges this. The initial rollout primarily targets institutional clients and high-net-worth users, who are more likely to value independent custody arrangements. Over time, Bitget hopes to simplify the process for smaller customers, potentially reducing the need to select and manage custodians individually. Importantly, participation is not intended to be mandatory. Customers would retain the option of keeping assets with Bitget or adopting the external custody model.

This raises a broader question for the industry. Can exchanges offer substantially stronger protection without sacrificing the simplicity that attracted users in the first place? Gracy believes the answer will depend on how effectively exchanges and custody providers develop the infrastructure together.

From Crypto's Original Ideals to Institutional Adoption

The discussion eventually moves beyond security to examine how cryptocurrency itself is evolving. Bitcoin emerged from a philosophy of decentralization, peer-to-peer transactions, and individual control over financial assets. Yet the industry now includes traditional financial institutions, investment products, and regulated intermediaries. Gracy doesn't necessarily see this as a contradiction.

She distinguishes decentralized blockchain networks from the institutions that provide access to assets operating on those networks. Bitcoin can remain decentralized even as banks, asset managers, and regulated exchanges participate in its broader ecosystem.
She points to the growing digital asset activities of institutions such as JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Fidelity as evidence of this transition. For Gracy, the industry is moving beyond its experimental years toward a stage where security, sustainable business models, and integration with traditional finance matter.

What Success Would Look Like

Gracy has a specific vision for measuring the Open Custody Network's success over the next three years. She wants at least half of Bitget's total assets under management to be held by independent custodians, with no custody-related security breaches and minimal disruption to the customer experience. She also hopes other centralized exchanges will adopt similar approaches.

Rather than positioning the network primarily as a new revenue opportunity, she describes it as an effort to encourage broader changes in how the industry manages security.
As crypto becomes part of a larger financial system, the industry must become more deliberate about who holds customer assets, how those assets are protected, and what risks users accept in exchange for convenience.

text:
Handwritten Early Draft of “Purple Rain” Lyrics Surfaces from Prince’s The Beautiful Ones

Sender: Prince (@prince)
Date: Wednesday, November 10, 2021
Time: 15:32 CET
Subject: Prince’s iconic “Purple Rain” began as a 13-minute live recording at First Avenue; this early handwritten lyric sheet from the book The Beautiful Ones shows an earlier draft.
Link: https://t.co/vJ64ad2gFT

On November 10, 2021, the official Prince account shared three images of a handwritten lyric sheet for the song that became one of the most enduring anthems in popular music. The post explained that “Purple Rain” was originally captured live at Minneapolis’s First Avenue club as a sweeping, roughly 13-minute performance and later edited down to the 8:41 version familiar from the 1984 album and film. The pages, drawn from the 2019 posthumous book The Beautiful Ones, offer a rare window into Prince’s early drafting process.

The August 3, 1983, benefit concert for the Minnesota Dance Theatre marked a pivotal night. Prince and the Revolution—featuring 19-year-old Wendy Melvoin’s live debut on guitar—debuted several new songs in front of an audience. A mobile recording truck from the Record Plant sat outside the club. Engineer David Z (David Rivkin) captured the show without the crowd knowing it would supply the basic tracks for the Purple Rain soundtrack. “Purple Rain,” “I Would Die 4 U,” and “Baby I’m a Star” all originated from that evening. Prince later trimmed the title track from about 13–14 minutes, overdubbed bass (the wireless signal had not recorded cleanly), and made other refinements while preserving the raw energy and the largely unrehearsed guitar solo. The result became the closing statement of an album that spent 24 consecutive weeks at number one.

The lyric sheet reveals material that did not survive into the finished song. One page opens with lines about never meaning to fill a life with sorrow or cause pain, then moves into a wish to see someone “bathing in the Purple Rain” and a chorus. Another section explores friendship versus weekend romance and the end of a bond. A second page contains more expansive, almost manifesto-like verses: “I don’t want money, I don’t want love. If I wanted either one, I would buy it. I want the heavy stuff. What your dreams are made of. I want control.” It also includes the striking self-description “I’m not a politician, I’m a purple musician,” and an invitation to trust and follow. The final page returns to the purple rain imagery with the promise “I only want to see u bathe in the Purple Rain.”

These discarded lines show Prince testing broader themes of leadership, desire, and transformation before distilling the song into its more concentrated form. In the released version, the purple rain functions as a potent metaphor for love, faith, and navigating the end of the world while remaining with the one you love. Prince once described the color combination of red and blue blood in the sky as the source of the title’s imagery.

The Beautiful Ones, edited by Dan Piepenbring, gathers Prince’s own handwritten memoir pages, early photos and scrapbooks, and materials related to the Purple Rain project, including these lyric drafts. The book preserves the artist’s distinctive cursive and the visible revisions—cross-outs, insertions, and alternative phrasings—that document how a landmark song took shape.

The official account’s post, which included the three pages, quickly drew fans who recognized the historical weight of both the live recording and the manuscript evidence. It stands as a concise reminder that even an iconic track began as a living, expandable performance and a set of evolving handwritten ideas.
#PrinceOnThisDay @prince

text:
Paisley Park Unveils Expanded Experiences and Merchandise One Month After Opening as Museum

Sender: Paisley Park (@PaisleyPark)
Date: November 10, 2016
Time: 22:20:32 GMT (4:20 PM CST)
Subject: N.E.W.S. for our purple Friends & Family: New #Experiences and New #Merchandise. #Prince
Link: https://t.co/K6bEbHvJ5Z

On November 10, 2016, roughly a month after Prince’s Chanhassen, Minnesota complex opened to the public as a museum on October 6, the official Paisley Park account shared news of expanded offerings for fans. The post, illustrated with a striking photo of Prince gazing from a window amid the building’s distinctive blue geometric architecture and skylights, directed purple friends and family to details on new experiences and merchandise.

The announcement aligned with a Business Wire release and coverage confirming that Paisley Park was adding tour dates through March 31, 2017, and launching themed packages starting December 1. Thursday VIP tours would let ticket holders record vocals over a short segment of a Prince song in the Studio B control room—the same space tied to hits from Sign o’ the Times, Graffiti Bridge, and Emancipation—and take home a live mix on USB. Fridays brought “Paisley Park After Dark” dance parties; Saturdays featured Prince movies and rare performance footage; Sundays offered a “Brunch Experience” with a meal in the NPG Music Club. These built on the initial general-admission ($38.50) and VIP ($100) guided tours that already showcased studios, the soundstage, wardrobe, instruments, awards, the Purple Rain motorcycle, and the atrium urn containing Prince’s ashes.

Merchandise updates accompanied the news, with online orders shipping to the USA, Canada, and Mexico (international shipping noted as coming soon). Items included apparel, totes, posters, and other memorabilia drawn from the archives, supporting the site’s operation under Graceland Holdings management amid ongoing rezoning for permanent daily access. The post captured the early momentum of preserving and sharing Prince’s creative sanctuary, where fans could step into the spaces that shaped his music and legacy.
